sections.name: Logical Reasoning
sections.description: Two scored sections on the LSAT (~24–26 questions each, 35 minutes per section). Each question presents a short argument or set of facts followed by a single multiple-choice prompt. LR tests the ability to analyze, evaluate, and complete arguments — the core daily work of a lawyer.
sections.format: ~25 standalone short-passage questions; 5 answer choices labeled A–E.
sections.scoring: Roughly 50% of the scaled score weight (two LR sections out of four scored sections).
skills: Spot reasoning flaws (causal, conditional, sampling, equivocation, …)
tips: Always identify the conclusion before evaluating the answers.
On flaw questions, name the flaw in your own words first.
Pre-phrase the right answer for assumption / strengthen / weaken before reading the choices.

sections.name: Reading Comprehension
sections.description: One scored section: four passages (one is typically a comparative pair) drawn from law, humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences, followed by 5–8 questions each. Tests close reading, structural mapping, and the ability to distinguish what the author claims from what the author merely reports.
sections.format: ~27 questions across 4 passage sets; 5 answer choices A–E.
sections.timing: 35 minutes total (~8:30 per passage including reading time).
sections.scoring: Roughly 25% of the scaled score weight.
skills: Identify main point, author attitude, and tone
Compare two passages on the comparative-reading set
tips: Read for STRUCTURE first, details second — questions reward knowing where to look.
Annotate authorship moves: claims, contrasts, examples, hedges.
Pre-phrase the main point before reading the answer choices.
Eliminate extremes for tone questions unless the passage is explicit.

sections.name: Analytical Reasoning (Logic Games)
sections.description: Historically four games per scored section (sequencing, grouping, matching, hybrid). LSAC announced a multi-year phase-out of the dedicated LG section beginning in August 2024 — replaced by an additional Logical Reasoning section on the August 2024 LSAT and beyond. Logic Games remain pedagogically essential: the diagramming skills they develop transfer directly to LR conditional reasoning and to legal exam writing. Practice them.
sections.format: Each game presents a setup + ~3–6 rules followed by 5–7 questions sharing the same setup; 5 answer choices A–E.
sections.scoring: Phasing out for the operational LSAT in 2024–2025; still scored on older PrepTests and many practice batteries.
tips: Spend the first 60–90 seconds turning the rules into a clean visual diagram.
On orientation questions, eliminate one answer per rule.
On 'if'-then questions, build the hypothetical and force every implication before reading the answers.
If you find more than two solutions for a 'must be true' question, you're missing an inference.

concepts.name: Alternative Cause
concepts.summary: A confounding variable that explains the observed pattern equally well or better.
concepts.detail: Most LR weaken answers introduce an alternative cause. Strengthen answers usually rule one out.

concepts.name: Appeal to Ignorance
concepts.summary: Treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence (or vice versa).
concepts.detail: 'No one has shown X is true, therefore X is false' — and its mirror 'No one has shown X is false, therefore X is true.' Both are flawed because lack of evidence settles nothing.

concepts.name: Author's Attitude / Tone
concepts.summary: Identify the author's stance toward the subject — endorsement, skepticism, neutrality, etc.
concepts.detail: Look for evaluative adjectives, hedge words ('arguably', 'risks'), and rhetorical questions. Hedged language usually means a hedged answer (qualified concern, cautious optimism) is right.

concepts.name: Causation vs. Correlation
concepts.summary: Inferring cause from a mere correlation is a classic LR flaw.
concepts.detail: When an argument says 'X and Y are correlated, therefore X causes Y', look for: (a) reverse causation (Y → X), (b) common cause (Z → both), (c) coincidence, (d) selection bias. Weaken answers usually surface one of these alternatives.
examples: Breakfast eaters score higher on cognitive tests → eating breakfast causes cognitive performance? Could be sleep, exercise, or socioeconomic confounders.

concepts.name: Conditional Reasoning
concepts.summary: Working with 'if/then' statements, their contrapositives, and chains of conditionals.
concepts.detail: Indicators: 'if', 'only if', 'unless', 'whenever', 'all', 'every', 'no', 'none'. 'Only if' attaches to the *necessary* condition; 'unless' translates to '¬X → Y'. Always diagram conditionals before answering and always check the contrapositive.
examples: Only members may vote → Vote → Member (and ¬Member → ¬Vote).
Unless you submit by Friday, your filing is late → ¬Submit-by-Friday → Late.

concepts.name: Contrapositive
concepts.summary: The contrapositive of 'P → Q' is '¬Q → ¬P'; logically equivalent.
concepts.detail: Contraposition is the workhorse of LR conditional questions. Note: the *converse* (Q → P) and the *inverse* (¬P → ¬Q) are NOT equivalent — confusing them is the affirming-the-consequent / denying-the-antecedent flaw.
examples: P → Q is equivalent to ¬Q → ¬P, but not to Q → P or ¬P → ¬Q.

concepts.name: Could Be True EXCEPT
concepts.summary: Four answers are possible in some valid layout; one is impossible. Pick the impossible.
concepts.detail: Treat as a 'must be false' question. Construct counter-examples for the four 'could' options; the remaining choice is your answer.

concepts.name: Detail Question
concepts.summary: Ask what the passage explicitly states. Always go back to the text.
concepts.detail: The right answer is paraphrased directly from a specific sentence; trap answers are inferences (correct, but not stated) or close-but-not-quite restatements.

concepts.name: Rule-Elimination
concepts.summary: Quickly knock out 'could be the order' answer choices by checking one rule at a time.
concepts.detail: On orientation questions, scan the answers rule-by-rule rather than building a master diagram. Each rule typically eliminates exactly one answer.

concepts.name: Equivocation
concepts.summary: Using one word in two different senses across an argument.
concepts.detail: Tricky because the equivocated term is often subtle ('volume of submissions' vs. 'diversity of viewpoints', or 'theory' as 'guess' vs. 'theory' as 'scientific framework'). Watch for shifts in scope between the premise and conclusion.

concepts.name: Flaw in the Reasoning
concepts.summary: Identify the logical error the argument commits.
concepts.detail: Common flaws: ad hominem, circular reasoning, equivocation, hasty generalization, sampling bias, appeal to ignorance, false dichotomy, conflating correlation with causation, part-whole conflations, conditional reasoning errors (affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent).

concepts.name: Grouping Game
concepts.summary: Select or distribute entities into groups under membership rules.
concepts.detail: Two families: selection (in/out of one group, e.g. 'choose four of seven') and distribution (partition into teams). Diagram membership conditionals ('If J is in, K is out' → J → ¬K) and chain contrapositives. Numeric limits (group sizes) drive most hard inferences.
examples: If J is selected then K is not; if K is not selected then L is. Selecting J forces L.

concepts.name: Main Conclusion
concepts.summary: Identify the statement the rest of the argument exists to support.
concepts.detail: The main conclusion is what everything else supports and what supports nothing further. Indicator words help ('therefore', 'thus') but the LSAT loves burying the conclusion first or mid-argument and decorating premises with conclusion-like language. Test a candidate by asking 'does anything in the argument support THIS?' — if yes, keep climbing.
examples: 'Since the statute is ambiguous, and ambiguous statutes are construed against the drafter, the clause should be read narrowly.' Main conclusion: read the clause narrowly.

concepts.name: Main Point Question
concepts.summary: Identify the central thesis of the passage.
concepts.detail: The main point summarizes the WHOLE passage, not a single paragraph. Wrong answers are usually too narrow (a single example) or too broad (a vague abstraction).

concepts.name: Method of Reasoning
concepts.summary: Describe HOW the argument proceeds, not whether it succeeds.
concepts.detail: Common techniques: counterexample, analogy, reductio ad absurdum, eliminating alternatives, appealing to a general principle, attacking a premise vs. attacking reasoning. The credited answer describes the move at the right abstraction level; traps describe techniques the argument never uses or misidentify the target of an objection.
examples: 'Opponents claim X; but X implies Y, and Y is absurd; so not-X' — a reductio.

concepts.name: Modus Ponens
concepts.summary: Valid conditional inference: if P then Q; P; therefore Q.
concepts.detail: The simplest valid conditional inference. Distinguish from the *invalid* mirror moves — affirming the consequent (Q ∴ P) and denying the antecedent (¬P ∴ ¬Q) — both classic LR flaw types.
examples: All senior partners have argued before the supreme court. Maria is a senior partner. ∴ Maria has argued before the supreme court.

concepts.name: Modus Tollens
concepts.summary: Valid conditional inference: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.
concepts.detail: Modus tollens is the contrapositive form. Whenever a conditional 'P → Q' is true, the contrapositive '¬Q → ¬P' is logically equivalent. The LSAT loves to test contrapositive recognition because students who only memorize 'P → Q' miss that the same rule also tells you what happens when Q fails.
examples: If the contract is enforceable, both parties signed. The contract was not signed by both parties. ∴ The contract is not enforceable.

concepts.name: Must Be True
concepts.summary: An answer that holds in every case consistent with the given statements.
concepts.detail: In LG: build the hypothetical, force every implication, then evaluate each answer — if even one valid layout makes the answer false, it doesn't 'must be true'. In LR: the credited inference must follow strictly from the stimulus; watch for quantifier downgrades ('all' → 'most' → 'some') and reversed conditionals in the traps.

concepts.name: Necessary Assumption
concepts.summary: An unstated premise the argument REQUIRES in order to hold.
concepts.detail: Use the negation test: negate the candidate; if the argument collapses, it was necessary. Necessary assumptions are minimally helpful — they fill the smallest possible gap, not the most ambitious.
examples: Argument: 'A or B; not A; ∴ B.' Necessary assumption: those were the only options.

concepts.name: Parallel Reasoning
concepts.summary: Match the abstract STRUCTURE of the stimulus, not its subject matter.
concepts.detail: Diagram the stimulus as variables (P, Q, R…). Then test each answer choice by diagramming it the same way. The correct answer must match the validity status (valid ↔ valid, invalid ↔ same kind of invalid) and the structural shape.

concepts.name: Principle Application
concepts.summary: Match a general rule to the concrete case that satisfies all of its conditions.
concepts.detail: Treat the principle as a conditional with (possibly several) trigger conditions and an exception clause. The conforming case satisfies every trigger and no exception. Traps satisfy most-but-not-all conditions, trip the exception, or run the principle backwards (concluding the trigger from the result).
examples: Principle: a lawyer may withdraw only if withdrawal will not prejudice the client. Case that conforms must show BOTH withdrawal AND no prejudice.

concepts.name: RC Inference
concepts.summary: What the passage most strongly supports beyond its explicit statements.
concepts.detail: Unlike detail questions, the credited answer is not stated — it follows from combining two or three passage claims. It stays modest: hedged language in the passage yields hedged inferences. Traps are real-world plausible but textually unsupported, or turn 'some commentators argue' into the author's own view.
examples: Passage: defenders cite discovery abuse; critics cite access. Supported inference: the parties disagree about which cost matters more — NOT that either side would abolish pleading standards.

concepts.name: Passage Structure
concepts.summary: Map each paragraph's role: setup, complication, evidence, counter-argument, resolution.
concepts.detail: Before answering questions, jot a one-line label for each paragraph. Most RC question types (main point, author attitude, role of statement, function of paragraph) become trivial once the structural map is clear.

concepts.name: Tone
concepts.summary: Closely related to author attitude — measure intensity (mild/strong) and polarity (positive/negative).
concepts.detail: Eliminate extremes ('uncritical', 'open hostility') unless the passage explicitly supports them.

concepts.name: Resolve the Paradox
concepts.summary: Find the fact that lets two apparently conflicting findings both be true.
concepts.detail: The stimulus reports a surprising discrepancy ('sales rose while ad spending fell'). The credited answer adds information that dissolves the tension without denying either finding. Wrong answers explain only one side, deepen the mystery, or drift out of scope.
examples: Fewer traffic tickets were issued, yet accident rates fell. Resolver: cameras replaced officers and deter violations without issuing tickets.

concepts.name: Sequencing Game
concepts.summary: Place items in a strict order (1st through nth) under constraints.
concepts.detail: Diagram with slots. Render rules as adjacency blocks (F-H), distance constraints, and forbidden positions. Make a hypothetical for any rule that creates few options.

concepts.name: Strengthen Question
concepts.summary: Pick the answer that, if true, most supports the argument.
concepts.detail: Mirror image of weaken: rule out alternative explanations, supply a missing assumption, or provide additional confirming evidence.

concepts.name: Sufficient Assumption
concepts.summary: An assumption strong enough to GUARANTEE the conclusion.
concepts.detail: Sufficient-assumption answers can be much stronger than necessary ones. The trick is to map the gap between premise and conclusion and find the answer that closes it completely.

concepts.name: Universal Instantiation
concepts.summary: From 'all P are Q' and 'x is P', conclude 'x is Q'. Always valid.
concepts.detail: The bedrock valid argument form. Distinguish from 'most P are Q' (probabilistic) and 'some P are Q' (existential).

concepts.name: Weaken Question
concepts.summary: Pick the answer that, if true, most undermines the argument.
concepts.detail: Identify the conclusion, then attack the link between premise and conclusion — typically by surfacing a counter-example, alternative cause, or unmet assumption. Avoid answers that simply contradict a premise (the LSAT treats premises as given).

passages.title: Five Associates, One Hearing
passages.summary: Sequencing game: order five associates in five consecutive slots subject to three rules.
passages.setup: Exactly five associates — F, G, H, J, and K — argue exactly one motion each at a single hearing. The motions are heard one at a time, in five consecutive time slots numbered 1 through 5 (1 is first, 5 is last). The order in which they argue is subject to the following constraints:

passages.title: Six Oral Arguments, One Morning
passages.summary: Sequencing game: order six moot-court students across six consecutive slots under two adjacency blocks and two ordering rules.
passages.setup: Exactly six students — F, G, H, J, K, and M — each present one oral argument at a moot-court program. The arguments are delivered one at a time, in six consecutive slots numbered 1 through 6 (1 is earliest, 6 is latest). No two arguments are delivered in the same slot. The order in which the students argue is subject to the following constraints:
rules: 3. K argues at some time before M.
4. F argues at some time before H.

passages.title: Six Witnesses, One Deposition
passages.summary: Sequencing game: order six witnesses across six consecutive deposition sessions under four rules; the constraints admit exactly four valid orders.
passages.setup: Exactly six witnesses -- L, M, N, P, R, and T -- are deposed, each testifying exactly once, in six consecutive sessions numbered 1 through 6 (1 is first, 6 is last). The order in which they testify is subject to the following constraints:
rules: 2. N testifies at some time before R.
4. L testifies either first or sixth.

passages.title: Six Paintings, One Gallery
passages.summary: Grouping/selection game: choose exactly three of six paintings to display under three conditional membership rules.
passages.setup: A museum curator must decide which paintings to hang in the main gallery. From six paintings — F, G, H, J, K, and L — the curator will display exactly three in the main gallery; the remaining three are placed in storage. The selection is governed by the following constraints:
rules: 1. If F is displayed, then H is displayed.
2. If G is displayed, then K is not displayed.
3. If H is displayed, then J is not displayed.

passages.title: From Code Pleading to Notice Pleading
passages.summary: A 4-paragraph excerpt on the evolution of federal civil procedure pleading standards.
passages.passage:
For most of the nineteenth century, common-law pleading required plaintiffs to fit their grievances into rigid formal categories — assumpsit, trespass on the case, trover. A misstep in selecting the proper writ could doom an otherwise meritorious claim. Reformers complained that the system rewarded procedural sophistication rather than substantive justice; the Field Code of 1848 in New York attempted a partial remedy by replacing the writ system with a unified civil action grounded in 'fact pleading.'

Fact pleading, however, generated its own pathologies. Courts disagreed about how granular the underlying facts had to be, and judges could dismiss a complaint for failing to plead a legally-significant element with sufficient specificity. By the 1930s a generation of procedural scholars — Charles Clark prominent among them — argued that the goal of pleading should be merely to give the defendant fair notice of the claim. The expensive work of testing factual sufficiency belonged in discovery and on summary judgment, not at the courthouse door.

This vision shaped the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, which took effect in 1938. Rule 8(a)(2)'s requirement of 'a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief' was a deliberate softening: the 1938 drafters knew they were trading some doctrinal predictability for procedural access. Conley v. Gibson (1957) cemented the bargain when the Supreme Court declared that a complaint should not be dismissed unless it was beyond doubt that no set of facts could support recovery.

The modern picture is more contested. Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly (2007) and Ashcroft v. Iqbal (2009) introduced a 'plausibility' threshold that some commentators read as a partial restoration of fact pleading. Defenders of the cases note that mass-tort and antitrust complaints had created discovery abuses the 1938 drafters could not have foreseen. Critics counter that the new standard risks reintroducing the very access barrier the 1938 drafters set out to dismantle, particularly for pro se litigants and civil-rights plaintiffs who often cannot satisfy plausibility without the discovery they are seeking.

passages.title: The Fall of the Privity Requirement
passages.summary: A 4-paragraph excerpt tracing American products-liability law from the privity bar through negligence to strict liability.
passages.passage:
Through most of the nineteenth century, a consumer injured by a defective product could rarely recover from its manufacturer. The doctrine of privity of contract, crystallized in the English case Winterbottom v. Wright (1842), held that a manufacturer's duty ran only to the party with whom it had directly contracted. A coachman maimed when a defective mail coach collapsed could not sue the supplier, because his employer, not he, had purchased the vehicle. Courts defended the rule as a necessary shield for a young industrial economy, reasoning that unlimited liability to remote users would chill manufacturing. The price of that protection fell on injured consumers, who were left without a remedy against the parties best positioned to prevent the harm.

The first decisive crack came in MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co. (1916). Writing for the New York Court of Appeals, Judge Benjamin Cardozo held that a manufacturer owes a duty of care to any foreseeable user of a product that is reasonably certain to place life and limb in peril when negligently made, regardless of privity. MacPherson did not abolish the need to prove fault; an injured plaintiff still had to show that the manufacturer had been negligent. But by untethering duty from the contract of sale, Cardozo reframed the question as one of foreseeability, and within two decades most American jurisdictions had followed.

Proving negligence, however, remained a formidable obstacle, since the relevant evidence usually lay in the manufacturer's exclusive control. In a celebrated 1944 concurrence in Escola v. Coca-Cola Bottling Co., Justice Roger Traynor urged courts to abandon fault altogether and hold manufacturers strictly liable for injuries caused by defective products. His view prevailed a generation later: Greenman v. Yuba Power Products (1963) imposed liability without proof of negligence, and the Restatement (Second) of Torts §402A (1965) codified strict liability for products sold in a defective condition unreasonably dangerous to the user. A plaintiff now needed to establish only a defect, causation, and injury.

Whether this represented a clean break is debatable. Strict liability was justified largely on the ground that manufacturers could spread the cost of injuries across all consumers through pricing and insurance — a rationale of risk distribution rather than moral fault. Yet in design-defect cases courts increasingly asked whether a product's risks outweighed its utility, an inquiry that looks suspiciously like the reasonableness balancing at the heart of negligence. The modern law of products liability thus sits uneasily between two theories, and its strict-liability label can obscure how much negligence reasoning survives within it.

passages.title: Proof by the Numbers: Statistics and the Burden of Proof
passages.summary: A 4-paragraph passage arguing that courts' resistance to naked statistical evidence reflects a demand for individualized, transparent proof rather than an aversion to numbers.
passages.passage:
Few questions divide evidence scholars as sharply as whether a naked statistical probability can, by itself, satisfy a legal burden of proof. Jurors reason quantitatively all the time — gauging how likely a witness is to be mistaken, or how probable an innocent explanation seems — yet courts grow uneasy the moment a party reduces that reasoning to an explicit number. The discomfort is not mere innumeracy. It reflects a durable intuition that a verdict must rest on evidence tying the defendant to this particular case, and not on a figure that would hold with equal force against anyone in a large class.

The canonical warning is People v. Collins. Prosecutors there multiplied together the estimated frequencies of several eyewitness details — a bearded man, a blond companion, a yellow car — to conclude that the odds of another couple matching the description were one in twelve million. An appellate court reversed the conviction, observing that the individual frequencies were never established by evidence and that multiplying them assumed, without proof, that each trait was statistically independent of the others. Collins is now cited less as a lesson about arithmetic than as a caution against the aura of certainty that a large number can lend to a shaky factual premise.

I share the courts' underlying instinct, though for a reason more principled than any distrust of mathematics. Consider the philosophers' gatecrasher hypothetical: one thousand people attend a rodeo, but only 499 bought tickets, so any given spectator is more likely than not to have entered without paying. Few of us would let the organizer collect from a randomly chosen attendee on that basis alone, even though the resulting 0.501 probability formally exceeds the civil 'preponderance' standard. What the naked number lacks is individualized proof — evidence about that spectator rather than about the crowd. The law's resistance, properly understood, defends this demand for particularized evidence; it is not a superstition about digits.

Yet the doctrine can curdle into reflexive hostility, and here the critics have a point. Courts today routinely admit DNA profiling, in which an analyst may testify that the chance of a random person matching the crime-scene sample is one in several billion. That figure is every bit as statistical as the one in Collins, but it is anchored to a transparent, replicable methodology and to a sample drawn from the defendant himself. The contrast shows that the objection was never to numbers as such. The principle worth keeping is the narrower one: quantified evidence earns its place when its method is auditable and its inference individualized — and forfeits that place when it is neither.

passages.title: From Riparian Right to Regulated Withdrawal
passages.summary: A 4-paragraph passage tracing water-allocation doctrine from common-law riparianism through prior appropriation to a defended synthesis, regulated riparianism.
passages.passage:
Under the common law of most humid regions, the right to use flowing water has long been tied to the ownership of land. The riparian doctrine grants each owner of land abutting a watercourse a correlative right to make reasonable use of the stream as it passes, subject to the like rights of every other riparian owner upstream and down. No one holds a superior claim by virtue of having used the water first, and no owner may so deplete or foul the flow as to defeat a neighbor's reasonable use. The doctrine's animating premise is sharing: because water in a well-watered landscape is rarely scarce enough to exhaust, the law can afford to treat it as a resource held in common by those the stream happens to touch.

That premise collapses in arid country. When the mining camps of the nineteenth-century American West confronted streams too meager to satisfy every claimant, a rule of sharing offered no guidance about who must go without. The doctrine of prior appropriation arose in answer. It severed water rights from land ownership entirely and awarded them instead to whoever first diverted the water and put it to a recognized beneficial use—irrigation, mining, municipal supply. 'First in time, first in right' meant that in a shortage the most senior appropriator took a full allotment while junior holders received nothing, a harshness the riparian system never contemplated. Whatever its rigor, the appropriation rule at least answered the question that scarcity forced and that riparianism could not.

Neither pure doctrine, I would argue, serves a modern jurisdiction well, and the more promising path is the regulated riparianism that a number of eastern states have quietly adopted. Under these regimes an administrative agency issues time-limited permits to withdraw water, allocating it by public criteria—the reasonableness of the use, its effect on the flow, the availability of alternatives—rather than by the accident of riverfront ownership or the brute priority of a diversion date. The permit system preserves riparianism's commitment to shared and reasonable use while supplying what the common law lacked: a forum for measuring competing demands against one another before a crisis, and a mechanism for adjusting allocations as conditions change.

The objection most often pressed against such systems is real. A permit regime substitutes the discretion of regulators for the predictability of a fixed rule, and an appropriator who has invested in reliance on a senior right may reasonably fear that a bureaucrat will unsettle it. I concede that predictability has genuine value, particularly where large capital investments depend on secure supply. But the certainty that prior appropriation offers is the certainty of a rule indifferent to changing needs, and the flexibility that regulated riparianism introduces is not lawlessness so long as the governing criteria are public and the agency's decisions are reviewable. On balance the trade favors regulation, because the scarcity that once afflicted only the arid West is fast becoming general.

passages.title: The Uses and Dangers of Legal Fictions
passages.summary: A 4-paragraph passage on legal fictions that contrasts Bentham's condemnation with Fuller's defense and argues their value depends on their remaining openly recognized as fictions.
passages.passage:
A legal fiction is an assertion that a court accepts as true, and proceeds to act upon, although everyone involved knows it to be false. Its purpose is practical: by pretending that some convenient state of affairs exists, a judge can escape a rule that would otherwise force an unjust or absurd result. Early common-law courts leaned on fictions chiefly to enlarge their own authority. The Court of King's Bench, for instance, could ordinarily try only prisoners already in its custody, so it invented the supposition that a defendant sued on an unrelated debt was being held on a fictitious trespass — a pretense that quietly extended the court's reach far beyond its original bounds. No statute authorized the maneuver; the fiction did the work that legislation might otherwise have required.

To Jeremy Bentham, this was precisely the scandal. Fictions, he argued, were instruments of judicial deceit: they allowed judges to change the law while pretending merely to apply it, and so to make binding rules without ever answering to the public in whose name they governed. A fiction, on Bentham's account, was always a confession of failure — proof that the written law had grown inadequate and that the bench was amending it in disguise. A properly codified legal system, drafted openly by a legislature, would dispense with fictions entirely; their persistence was a symptom of arrested legal development, not a sign of judicial ingenuity.

Writing a century later, Lon Fuller declined to join in the condemnation. Fuller drew a line between fictions that deceive and fictions that merely express — a compressed shorthand for a legal relationship the law has not yet learned to name directly. The description of a corporation as a 'person,' on this reading, asserts no falsehood; it states economically that the entity holds rights and bears duties of its own. Fuller conceded that a fiction can curdle into dogma: later readers may forget the silent 'as if' and mistake the metaphor for a fact about the world. Yet the hazard, he maintained, lies in that forgetting, not in the fiction itself, which at its birth is merely an honest device for saying something new.

The better view leans toward Fuller, but with a qualification he left underdeveloped: a fiction is worth its cost only so long as it remains visible as a fiction. Labeled plainly, it advertises the gap between existing doctrine and present need, and thereby invites the very reform Bentham wanted. Left to harden, it does the opposite — it buries a contestable policy choice beneath the appearance of settled truth, so that no one thinks to revisit it. Bentham's alarm, then, is not baseless; it simply misidentifies the culprit. The danger is not the device but the profession's habit of mistaking a useful metaphor for a discovery. The soundest fictions are the ones that announce their own eventual obsolescence.

passages.title: Scoring Risk: Actuarial Instruments in Bail and Sentencing
passages.summary: A 4-paragraph passage arguing that actuarial risk-assessment instruments, though a plausible corrective to biased judicial discretion, have been adopted faster than the transparency and validation safeguards they require.
passages.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, a judge deciding whether to release a defendant before trial or how long to incarcerate one after conviction relied on little more than the case file and a practiced sense of the person in front of the bench. That intuition was famously uneven: two defendants with nearly identical records could receive markedly different treatment depending on the courtroom they happened to draw. Into this gap stepped the actuarial risk-assessment instrument, a statistical tool that assigns each defendant a numerical score estimating the likelihood of rearrest. Marketed as a corrective to human caprice, such instruments now inform bail and sentencing decisions in jurisdictions across the country.

The case for these tools is not frivolous, and I do not dismiss it. A well-validated instrument can flag patterns that an overworked judge, reasoning case by case, will miss; it can also impose a welcome consistency, ensuring that similarly situated defendants are scored by the same yardstick rather than by the vagaries of an individual temperament. Proponents point out, fairly, that the alternative is not some pristine neutrality but the very discretionary judgment whose documented disparities prompted reform in the first place. If the choice is between unexamined intuition and a transparent formula, the formula would seem the safer bet.

Yet the formula is rarely transparent, and this is where my confidence falters. Many widely used instruments are proprietary, their inner workings shielded from the defendants they score and even from the courts that rely on them. More troubling still is what the instruments measure. Because direct predictors of rearrest are scarce, developers lean on proxies—residential stability, employment history, the arrest records of family members—that track socioeconomic disadvantage and, through it, race. A score that appears to describe an individual's dangerousness may in fact encode the circumstances of the neighborhood he was born into, laundering old inequities through the authority of a number.

None of this makes the instruments worthless, and I resist the temptation to condemn them wholesale. Used as one input among many, subjected to independent validation, and stripped of the proxies most likely to smuggle in bias, they might yet deliver the consistency their designers promise. My reservation is narrower but firm: the pace of adoption has badly outrun the development of these safeguards. Until transparency and testing catch up, a tool sold as a remedy for arbitrary judgment risks becoming a more durable, and less accountable, form of it.

passages.title: The Reasonable Person and the Allocation of Risk
passages.summary: A 4-paragraph argument that the objective reasonable-person standard in negligence is best defended not as a moral verdict on the defendant but as a pragmatic device for allocating the risks of human variation.
passages.passage:
Negligence law asks whether a defendant exercised the care a 'reasonable person' would have shown under the circumstances. The formula is deliberately objective: the jury measures the defendant's conduct against an external community standard rather than against the defendant's own capacities, intentions, or best efforts. A driver who genuinely tried to be careful is nonetheless liable if a reasonable driver would have done more. For more than a century this impersonal yardstick has been the organizing device of accident law, and its very abstractness — its refusal to ask what this particular defendant could manage — is what makes it administrable across the endless variety of cases that juries confront.

To many critics the standard's impersonality is precisely its vice. Ordinary morality, they observe, excuses those who do the best they can: we do not blame a person of limited intelligence for failing to foresee a danger that a cleverer person would have caught. Yet negligence law holds the slow-witted, the inexperienced, and the congenitally clumsy to the same external measure as everyone else, condemning them for shortcomings they could not have overcome. On this view the reasonable-person test punishes people not for choosing badly but for being who they are, substituting a verdict about capacity for the moral judgment about choice that liability is supposed to express.

This objection, I want to suggest, misconceives what the standard is for. The reasonable-person test is not a covert assessment of the defendant's character or a pronouncement that she is a bad person; it is a rule for allocating the risk created by human variation. Someone whose reflexes or judgment fall below the community's ordinary expectations imposes an above-ordinary hazard on everyone she encounters, and the law sensibly places the cost of that hazard on the person who introduces it rather than on the strangers who cannot anticipate it. Read this way, the standard's refusal to individualize is not a moral blindness but a considered decision about who should bear the price of unusual limitations.

None of this is to deny that the objective standard has soft edges. Courts do individualize in limited ways — they hold children to the conduct of children of like age and experience, and they excuse the driver felled by a sudden, unforeseeable stroke. These carve-outs might seem to concede the critics' premise, but they in fact confirm the allocative logic: the law relaxes the standard only where insisting on it would place risk on someone who neither created it nor could guard against it. The reasonable person, in short, is best understood not as a moral ideal we all fall short of, but as a pragmatic instrument for distributing the unavoidable costs of living among the imperfect.

questions.stem:
Every senior partner at the firm has argued at least one case before the state supreme court. Maria is a senior partner at the firm. Therefore, Maria has argued at least one case before the state supreme court.

The argument above is most similar in its reasoning to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All birds have feathers. A penguin is a bird. So a penguin has feathers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most lawyers own at least one suit. Therefore, the lawyer next door owns a suit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who passed the bar studied. Tom studied, so Tom passed the bar.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If it rains, the picnic is canceled. The picnic was canceled, so it rained.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No senator is under 30. Lin is 28, so Lin might be a senator.

questions.explanation: The original is a valid universal-instantiation argument: 'All P are Q; x is P; therefore x is Q.' Choice A has identical form. B uses 'most' (probabilistic). C affirms the consequent. D denies the antecedent reversed. E contradicts a universal.

questions.stem:
City planner: Building a light-rail line will reduce traffic congestion downtown, because every comparable city that built one saw congestion fall within five years.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The light-rail line will be more expensive than the planner estimates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some downtown residents oppose the construction noise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Light-rail riders in those cities reported high satisfaction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The comparable cities all simultaneously enacted downtown congestion-pricing tolls.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proposed line will run mostly underground.

questions.explanation: The argument infers causation from correlation across comparable cities. D introduces a confound — congestion-pricing tolls — that may explain the congestion drop instead of the rail line, undermining the causal inference. A attacks cost (irrelevant to congestion). B, C, and E are off-point.

questions.stem:
If the contract is enforceable, then it was signed by both parties. The contract was not signed by both parties.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contract is enforceable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contract is not enforceable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contract is partially enforceable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only one party intended to be bound.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nothing can be concluded about enforceability.

questions.explanation: Modus tollens: 'If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.' If enforceable required both signatures and we lack both signatures, the contract is not enforceable. The other options either affirm the consequent, add facts not given, or reject a valid inference.

questions.stem:
Editor: Our new policy requires every opinion piece to cite at least three primary sources. Critics claim this will reduce the diversity of viewpoints we publish, since fewer freelance writers have access to primary sources. But our submission rate has not dropped since the policy took effect, so the critics are mistaken.

The editor's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a necessary condition as if it were sufficient.

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes without warrant that all freelance writers lack primary sources.

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that some published pieces cite more than three sources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers a general rule from a single anecdote.

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the volume of submissions with the diversity of viewpoints in those submissions.

questions.explanation: The critics' claim is about *diversity of viewpoints*. The editor rebuts using *submission volume*. Equating the two is the flaw — submission count and viewpoint diversity are different measures, so E names it. A, B, C, and D mischaracterize the structure.

questions.stem:
Studies show that people who eat breakfast perform better on cognitive tests in the morning than people who skip breakfast. Therefore, eating breakfast causes improved cognitive performance.

The argument's reasoning is flawed because it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on studies that may not be representative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to specify what counts as breakfast.

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers causation from correlation without ruling out alternative explanations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that all cognitive tests measure the same ability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: ignores that some people perform well without breakfast.

questions.explanation: Classic correlation ≠ causation flaw. People who eat breakfast may also sleep more, exercise, or have less stress — any of which could be the real cause. The argument fails to rule out these confounders. A, B, D, E are peripheral.

questions.stem:
Columnist: Supporters of the new zoning ordinance say it will preserve the neighborhood's historic character. But the supporters have not produced any architectural surveys to back up that claim. So the ordinance will not preserve the historic character.

The columnist's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: presupposes what it sets out to prove.

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on a sample that is too small.

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about an individual from claims about a group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats absence of evidence as evidence of absence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: appeals to popular opinion rather than to facts.

questions.explanation: Lack of supporting evidence does not establish the opposite conclusion (the ordinance might still preserve the character even if no survey has been produced). This appeal-to-ignorance flaw is captured by D. A, B, C, and E describe errors the columnist did not commit.

questions.stem:
Lawyer: To win the appeal, the defendant must show either that the trial court misapplied the statute or that the jury was improperly instructed. The trial court did not misapply the statute. So if the defendant wins the appeal, then the jury was improperly instructed.

The lawyer's reasoning depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There are no other grounds on which the appeal could be won.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The defendant will win the appeal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Showing improper jury instructions is sufficient to win an appeal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The jury was in fact improperly instructed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Misapplication of the statute would have been the stronger ground.

questions.explanation: The argument lists two ways to win and rules one out, then concludes the other must be the route to a win. That move only works if those two were the *only* possible grounds. Choice A makes that necessary assumption explicit. B, C, D, and E add facts the argument neither states nor requires.

questions.stem:
Researcher: Patients who received the new therapy recovered faster than those who received the standard treatment. So the new therapy must be more effective than the standard treatment.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new therapy is more expensive than the standard treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some patients given the standard treatment also recovered quickly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two groups of patients were similar in age, overall health, and severity of illness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The researcher has studied the standard treatment for many years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A few patients given the new therapy reported mild side effects.

questions.explanation: Moving from 'recovered faster' to 'more effective' assumes the two groups were comparable to begin with. C rules out the alternative that the new-therapy group was simply healthier, strengthening the causal claim. A and E raise cost and side-effects, which are irrelevant to effectiveness. B and D neither support nor close the gap.

questions.stem:
Only employees who completed the safety course may operate the forklift. No temporary worker has completed the safety course.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some temporary workers may operate the forklift.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every employee who completed the safety course operates the forklift.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who operates the forklift is a temporary worker.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Completing the safety course is sufficient to be allowed to operate the forklift.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No temporary worker may operate the forklift.

questions.explanation: 'Only those who completed the course may operate' means operating requires completion (operate → completed). The contrapositive is ¬completed → ¬operate. Since no temporary worker completed the course, no temporary worker may operate the forklift — E. A contradicts this. B and D treat a necessary condition as if it were sufficient. C reverses the conditional.

questions.stem:
Critic: If a film is a commercial success, it will be widely imitated. This year's top-grossing comedy has already spawned a dozen imitators. So it was a commercial success.

The critic's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes a condition that guarantees an outcome to be required for that outcome.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a result that the premise says would follow from success as if it established success.

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on a sample of films that is too small to support a generalization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that what is true of one comedy is true of all comedies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the popularity of a film with its artistic merit.

questions.explanation: The premise says success → imitation. The critic observes imitation and infers success, affirming the consequent — imitation could arise for other reasons. B names this error. A describes the converse mistake (necessary vs. sufficient) the critic did not make. C, D, and E raise issues the argument does not turn on.

questions.stem:
Anyone who understands the proof will pass the exam. Therefore, Dana will pass the exam.

The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dana understands the proof.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dana has studied harder than anyone else in the class.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Everyone who passes the exam understands the proof.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most students who understand the proof pass the exam.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Anyone who passes the exam will later understand the proof.

questions.explanation: This is a sufficient-assumption question: find the premise that, added to 'understands the proof → passes the exam,' guarantees the conclusion that Dana passes. Only A does it — if Dana understands the proof, the rule forces the conclusion that Dana passes. B is irrelevant (studying is not the stated trigger). D is merely probabilistic ('most'), so it cannot guarantee the result. C and E reverse the conditional (pass → understand), which never licenses concluding that Dana passes.

questions.stem:
If the witness is credible, then the alibi holds. If the alibi holds, then the defendant was not at the scene. The witness is credible.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The defendant was not at the scene.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The alibi does not hold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The witness is not credible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the defendant was not at the scene, then the witness is credible.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The defendant was at the scene.

questions.explanation: Chain the conditionals — credible → alibi holds → not at scene — and apply modus ponens to the given fact that the witness is credible. The conclusion that follows is that the defendant was not at the scene (A). B and C contradict the premises. D reverses a conditional (affirming the consequent) and is not guaranteed. E directly contradicts the valid conclusion.

questions.stem:
If a witness is impeached with a prior inconsistent statement, then the witness's credibility is called into question. Officer Reyes was impeached with a prior inconsistent statement during cross-examination.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded on the basis of the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Officer Reyes's testimony will be excluded from evidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Officer Reyes's credibility has been called into question.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any witness whose credibility is called into question has been impeached with a prior inconsistent statement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A witness who is not impeached with a prior inconsistent statement will not have his credibility called into question.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It cannot be determined whether Officer Reyes's credibility has been called into question.

questions.explanation: B follows by modus ponens: the conditional's antecedent (impeachment with a prior inconsistent statement) is satisfied by Officer Reyes, so the stated consequent (credibility called into question) must hold. A introduces exclusion of testimony, a consequence the stimulus never mentions, so it is out of scope. C commits the converse, wrongly assuming impeachment by prior inconsistent statement is the only way credibility could be questioned. D commits the inverse, wrongly inferring that failing to satisfy the antecedent guarantees the consequent fails too. E wrongly denies that a determinate conclusion is available, when modus ponens settles the matter with certainty.

questions.stem:
If an appellate brief exceeds the court's page limit, then the clerk will reject the filing. The defendant's appellate brief exceeds the court's page limit.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded on the basis of the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any brief that the clerk rejects must exceed the court's page limit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A brief that does not exceed the court's page limit will not be rejected by the clerk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cannot be determined whether the clerk will reject the defendant's brief.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The clerk will reject the defendant's brief.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The defendant's brief also fails to comply with the court's formatting requirements.

questions.explanation: D follows by modus ponens: exceeding the page limit is sufficient to trigger rejection, and the defendant's brief satisfies that antecedent, so rejection must follow. A commits the converse, treating rejection as proof that a brief exceeded the limit, when the stimulus never states that exceeding the limit is the only route to rejection. B commits the inverse, wrongly assuming that not triggering the rule guarantees the opposite outcome. C wrongly denies that a valid inference is available, when modus ponens settles it. E introduces an unstated defect (formatting) the stimulus never mentions, so it is out of scope.

questions.stem:
If a title company fails to record a deed within thirty days of closing, then the buyer's claim to the property loses priority over later recorded claims. The title company handling Ms. Alvarez's purchase failed to record her deed within thirty days of closing.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded on the basis of the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ms. Alvarez's claim to the property loses priority over later recorded claims.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any buyer whose claim loses priority had a title company that failed to record the deed within thirty days.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A buyer whose deed is recorded within thirty days will never lose priority to a later recorded claim.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether Ms. Alvarez's claim loses priority cannot be determined from the information given.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ms. Alvarez is entitled to sue the title company for damages.

questions.explanation: A is the direct modus ponens conclusion: the rule's trigger (failure to record within thirty days) is satisfied, so the stated consequence (loss of priority) must follow. B commits the converse, assuming late recording is the only route to losing priority. C commits the inverse, wrongly assuming that satisfying a different condition (timely recording) guarantees the opposite outcome, something the stimulus never claims. D wrongly treats the conclusion as indeterminate when modus ponens makes it certain. E introduces a remedy (a damages suit) never discussed in the stimulus, so it is out of scope.

questions.stem:
If an employee discloses a trade secret to a competitor, then the employee breaches the confidentiality agreement. Deshawn, an employee at Havelock Robotics, disclosed a trade secret to a competitor.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded on the basis of the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any employee who breaches the confidentiality agreement has disclosed a trade secret to a competitor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An employee who does not disclose a trade secret to a competitor will not breach the confidentiality agreement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether Deshawn breached the confidentiality agreement cannot be determined from the information given.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deshawn will likely be terminated from his position at Havelock Robotics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deshawn breached the confidentiality agreement.

questions.explanation: E follows by modus ponens: disclosing a trade secret to a competitor is sufficient to trigger a breach, and Deshawn did exactly that, so the breach must follow. A commits the converse, assuming disclosure to a competitor is the only way to breach the agreement. B commits the inverse, wrongly inferring that not disclosing to a competitor guarantees no breach. C wrongly denies that the conclusion can be determined, when modus ponens settles it with certainty. D introduces an unstated consequence (termination) that the stimulus never addresses, making it out of scope.

questions.stem:
If a document is to be admitted as a valid affidavit, then it must be signed in the presence of a notary. This document was not signed in the presence of a notary.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded from the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The document was signed in the presence of a witness who is not a notary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The document cannot be admitted as a valid affidavit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The document was admitted as a valid affidavit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a document is signed in the presence of a notary, then it may be admitted as a valid affidavit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No conclusion can be drawn about whether the document is a valid affidavit.

questions.explanation: The rule given is 'if a document is to be admitted as a valid affidavit (P), it must be signed before a notary (Q),' paired with the negated consequent: this document was not signed before a notary (not-Q). Modus tollens licenses the negated antecedent: the document cannot be admitted as a valid affidavit, choice B. A introduces a fact never supplied by the stimulus — whether any other witness was present is simply unknown. C asserts P, the exact opposite of the guaranteed conclusion; the negated consequent rules P out rather than supporting it. D states the converse of the original rule, swapping which condition is sufficient and which is necessary; nothing in the stimulus establishes that being notarized is sufficient for admissibility. E wrongly claims no conclusion is available, but modus tollens makes B a certain, valid inference from the two given statements.

questions.stem:
If a notice of appeal is filed on time, then the appellate court will have jurisdiction to hear the case. The appellate court does not have jurisdiction to hear this case.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded from the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The appellate court has jurisdiction to hear the case.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The notice of appeal was filed on time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the appellate court has jurisdiction to hear a case, then the notice of appeal in that case was filed on time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The notice of appeal was not filed on time.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether the notice of appeal was filed on time cannot be determined from the statements above.

questions.explanation: The rule given is 'if filed on time (P), then the court has jurisdiction (Q),' and we're told the court lacks jurisdiction (not-Q). Modus tollens converts this negated consequent into the negated antecedent: the notice was not filed on time, choice D. A asserts Q — that the court has jurisdiction — which directly contradicts the stimulus's second sentence. B asserts P, the reverse of the valid conclusion; the negated consequent rules P out rather than supporting it. C states the converse of the original rule, treating jurisdiction as though it guarantees timely filing; the stimulus never licenses that reversed relationship. E incorrectly denies that any conclusion can be drawn, but the negated consequent guarantees D by modus tollens.

questions.stem:
No conclusive study has ever shown that the herbal supplement Vitalex causes liver damage. Therefore, Vitalex is safe for long-term use.

The argument's reasoning is questionable because it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on the personal testimony of Vitalex users rather than controlled data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: attacks the credibility of scientists who have criticized Vitalex.

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to specify what would count as "long-term use."

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the absence of proof that Vitalex is harmful as proof that it is safe.

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws its conclusion from a study population that may be too small to detect rare side effects.

questions.explanation: The argument moves directly from 'no study has proven Vitalex causes harm' to 'Vitalex is safe,' which is the appeal-to-ignorance flaw named in D: absence of proof of harm is not proof of safety -- it may simply mean the right study hasn't been done yet. A is wrong because the argument never mentions user testimony; it cites the absence of studies, not personal accounts. B is wrong because the argument never disputes anyone's credibility -- it doesn't engage with critics at all. C is a red herring: the term 'long-term use' is not what makes the inference weak; the inference fails regardless of how that phrase is defined. E misdescribes the argument, which rests on the total absence of confirming studies, not on a specific study's sample size -- no such study is discussed. D alone captures the actual gap between the premise and the conclusion.

questions.stem:
Auditors found no documentation proving that Meridian Consulting overbilled its clients last year. City officials therefore concluded that Meridian did not overbill its clients.

The city officials' reasoning is flawed because it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the absence of documentation proving overbilling as proof that no overbilling occurred.

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes that all consulting firms behave the same way when it comes to billing practices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: questions the auditors' competence rather than addressing the substance of their findings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to define what conduct would count as "overbilling."

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on a single year's audit to draw a conclusion about the firm's overall practices.

questions.explanation: The officials infer 'no overbilling occurred' solely from 'no documentation proves it occurred' -- but missing proof of overbilling is not proof of its absence; the documentation might simply not exist or might not have been found. A states this precisely. B is wrong because the argument makes no claim about consulting firms generally -- it is confined to Meridian. C is wrong because the argument never disputes the auditors' competence; it accepts their findings and misinterprets what those findings show. D is a red herring: however 'overbilling' is defined, the inference from 'no proof found' to 'none occurred' is equally unsupported. E is wrong because the argument's flaw is not about how much data was examined but about what conclusion an absence of evidence licenses; the single-year scope is not what makes the inference fail. Only A identifies the actual gap.

questions.stem:
In Rivertown, every building permit application is reviewed by the planning board. Any application reviewed by the planning board that proposes a structure taller than 40 feet is also referred to the historic commission. The application for the Elm Street project proposes a structure that is 55 feet tall.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Elm Street application will be referred to the historic commission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Elm Street application will be approved by the historic commission.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only applications proposing structures taller than 40 feet are referred to the historic commission.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the Elm Street project's height is reduced to 35 feet, the application will not be referred to the historic commission.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The planning board reviewed the Elm Street application before its height reached 55 feet.

questions.explanation: A is correct: every application is reviewed by the planning board (so Elm Street's is), and any reviewed application proposing a structure over 40 feet is referred to the historic commission; since Elm Street proposes 55 feet, referral follows from two applications of the given rules. B claims approval, but referral to a body is not the same as approval by it -- a scope shift beyond what is stated. C illegitimately converts the sufficient condition (over 40 feet triggers referral) into a necessary one, asserting no other route to referral could exist -- unsupported. D reasons from an unaddressed hypothetical height change and wrongly assumes the 40-foot threshold is the only possible trigger; this denies the antecedent invalidly. E introduces an unsupported temporal detail about timing that the stimulus never discusses.

questions.stem: Although rising interest rates have slowed home sales nationwide, the downtown condominium market here should be classified as healthy rather than declining. Sales data show that condominiums priced below $400,000 continue to sell within two weeks of listing, since first-time buyers view them as an affordable alternative to renting. Furthermore, developers are still breaking ground on three new condo towers this year, a sign of confidence that would make little sense in a genuinely declining market.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rising interest rates have slowed home sales nationwide.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The downtown condominium market here should be regarded as healthy, not declining.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Condominiums priced below $400,000 sell within two weeks of being listed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: First-time buyers view condominiums under $400,000 as an affordable alternative to renting.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Developers would not break ground on new towers in a market that is genuinely declining.

questions.explanation: The conclusion, tucked into the sentence right after the concession, is that the downtown condo market should be seen as healthy rather than declining -- everything else in the stimulus supports that claim, so B restates it correctly. A merely restates the concession about interest rates, which the author grants before pivoting to disagree; it is the point conceded, not the point argued. C reports the fast-selling-condo data, a premise offered as evidence, not the claim being defended. D gives the reason (via 'since') for why cheaper condos sell quickly -- a premise one level further down, easy to mistake for the point because of its confident, explanatory phrasing. E restates the developer-confidence premise, which supports the conclusion but is not itself what the argument sets out to establish.

questions.stem:
Historians have never found any document proving that the ancient city of Kallira lacked a functioning irrigation system. Therefore, Kallira must have had a functioning irrigation system.

The historians' reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: assumes that every ancient city needed an irrigation system to survive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on the testimony of historians who may be biased toward a particular theory of Kallira's history.

choices.label: C
choices.text: concludes that a claim is true merely because no evidence has been found to refute it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to define what would count as a "functioning" irrigation system.

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizes from the practices of one ancient city to ancient cities generally.

questions.explanation: The argument's only support for 'Kallira had irrigation' is that no document disproves it -- but a missing disproof is not proof of truth; the relevant records may simply be lost or never written. That is exactly the error C names. A is wrong because the argument never claims irrigation was necessary for survival -- it just asserts Kallira had one. B mischaracterizes the argument: no historian's testimony or bias is invoked, only the absence of a document. D is a red herring -- however 'functioning' is defined, the inference from 'no disproof' to 'true' remains equally weak. E is wrong because the argument draws no conclusion about other ancient cities at all; it stays narrowly focused on Kallira. Only C identifies the genuine gap between premise and conclusion.

questions.stem:
Since no employee has ever filed a formal complaint about the safety of the new assembly-line robots, the robots must pose no safety risk to workers.

The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: questions the motives of employees who might raise safety concerns.

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes that employees would report a real safety risk if one existed, rather than establishing that no risk exists.

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on too short an operating history to rule out rare mechanical failures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to specify what would count as a "safety risk."

choices.label: E
choices.text: compares the robots to a different, unrelated type of machinery.

questions.explanation: The argument treats the absence of complaints as if it settles the question of danger, but silence could mean many things besides safety -- workers may not notice a risk, may fear retaliation, or may not know how to file a complaint. B names this: the argument merely assumes complaints would occur if risk existed, rather than showing risk is actually absent. A is wrong because the argument never questions any employee's motives -- it simply notes an absence of complaints. C is a sample-size-style distractor that doesn't apply here: the argument's flaw is treating silence as proof, not relying on a short observation window, which is not mentioned. D is a red herring -- no matter how 'safety risk' is defined, the leap from 'no complaints' to 'no risk' remains unjustified. E is wrong because the argument makes no comparison to any other machinery. B alone captures the appeal-to-ignorance gap.

questions.stem: Principle: A retailer may decline to complete a sale at an item's posted price only if (1) the posted price is so far below the item's evident value that no reasonable shopper could believe it reflects the retailer's intended price, and (2) the retailer informs the shopper of the pricing error before the sale is finalized. Which of the following situations conforms to this principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A jewelry store had priced a diamond ring at $19.99 instead of $1,999.00. A customer purchased the ring and the sale was completed; only afterward did the store call the customer to explain the labeling error and ask that the ring be returned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A furniture store had priced a leather sofa at $45 instead of $4,500 because of a decimal-point error. Before ringing up the sale, the cashier told the customer about the error and declined to sell the sofa for $45.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A bookstore priced a novel at $8, well below its usual $25, as part of an intentional clearance sale. Midway through the transaction, the manager decided she would rather not sell it that cheaply and told the customer before completing the sale.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An electronics store had priced a laptop at $4 instead of $400 because of a scanner glitch. The clerk noticed the obvious error, canceled the transaction without explanation, and said nothing to the confused customer about why.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A grocery store had correctly priced milk at $3.79. A new cashier mistakenly believed this was a pricing error and, before completing the sale, told the customer she would not honor what she wrongly took to be a mispriced item.

questions.explanation: The principle requires BOTH that the price be so obviously wrong no reasonable shopper could think it intended, AND that the retailer notify the shopper before the sale is finalized. B satisfies both: the $45 sofa price is an obvious decimal error, and the cashier disclosed it and declined before completing the sale -- this is the credited answer. A meets condition (1) but violates condition (2)'s timing: notice came after the sale was completed, not before. C fails condition (1): an intentional clearance markdown is not an obvious pricing error, so the retailer had no principle-based license to back out. D meets condition (1) but fails condition (2): the store never informed the customer of the error at all. E fails condition (1): the milk was priced correctly, so there was no error to invoke, regardless that notice was given before the sale.

questions.stem:
If a shipment passes customs inspection, it is released to the distributor. Every shipment either passes customs inspection or fails it. Any shipment that fails customs inspection is flagged for a compliance review. The shipment from Pier 12 was not released to the distributor.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shipment from Pier 12 passed customs inspection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every shipment that is flagged for compliance review failed customs inspection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The shipment from Pier 12 was flagged for compliance review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The shipment from Pier 12 will eventually be released to the distributor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only shipments from Pier 12 are flagged for compliance review.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Since the shipment was not released, the contrapositive of the first rule shows it did not pass inspection; because every shipment either passes or fails, it therefore failed, and the third rule then requires that it be flagged for compliance review. A directly contradicts this modus tollens result. B converts the one-directional rule 'fails, therefore flagged' into its converse 'flagged, therefore failed,' and further overgeneralizes it to every shipment ever flagged. D asserts an eventual release that nothing in the stimulus supports -- the shipment has already been established as not released, and no timeline is given. E takes a fact about one shipment and unjustifiably restricts flagging to shipments from that single pier.

questions.stem:
If a manuscript is accepted for publication, it has passed peer review. Any manuscript that has passed peer review does not contain plagiarized material. It has been confirmed that the manuscript submitted by Chen contains plagiarized material.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chen's manuscript passed peer review.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every manuscript that contains plagiarized material is rejected outright.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If Chen's manuscript had not contained plagiarized material, it would have been accepted for publication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The plagiarized material in Chen's manuscript was discovered during peer review.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chen's manuscript was not accepted for publication.

questions.explanation: E is correct. The second rule's contrapositive shows that any manuscript containing plagiarized material has not passed peer review; the first rule's contrapositive then shows that any manuscript that has not passed peer review was not accepted for publication. Chaining these through Chen's manuscript yields that it was not accepted. A directly contradicts this chain. B overgeneralizes from Chen's single manuscript to a universal claim about all manuscripts, and asserts an outcome ('rejected outright') never mentioned in the stimulus. C mistakes the absence of plagiarism for a sufficient condition for acceptance, when the stimulus only makes passing peer review necessary for acceptance. D introduces an unsupported claim about when and how the plagiarism was discovered.

questions.stem: Some parents argue that youth chess leagues are not worth the cost because few participants become professional players. Still, local youth chess leagues deserve continued funding, since players consistently show measurable gains in concentration and planning skills that carry over into schoolwork. These cognitive gains, moreover, tend to persist for years after a child stops playing competitively, since the strategic habits chess builds become part of how a child approaches any complex problem.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Few participants in youth chess leagues go on to become professional players.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Youth chess players show measurable gains in concentration and planning skills that carry over into schoolwork.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cognitive gains from playing youth chess tend to persist for years after a child stops competing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Local youth chess leagues deserve continued funding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The strategic habits chess builds become part of how a child approaches any complex problem.

questions.explanation: The author concedes that few players turn pro but pivots with 'Still' to argue that funding should continue -- that claim, D, is the main conclusion, and everything after it is evidence for it. A merely repeats the conceded point used to open the opposing view, not the author's own claim. B cites the concentration-and-planning-skills data, the first piece of support, introduced by 'since' -- a premise, not the point being proved. C reports a second premise, that the gains persist for years, again offered as evidence for continued funding rather than as the funding claim itself. E goes one level deeper still, explaining why the gains persist; it supports C, which in turn supports D, making it a premise twice removed from the conclusion.

questions.stem: Some managers concede that fully remote employees report higher job satisfaction than their in-office peers. Nevertheless, the firm should not extend its remote-work pilot program to additional departments, because departments that shifted to remote work last year saw a measurable decline in cross-team collaboration, and because that decline in collaboration preceded a slowdown in the firm's product-development timeline. A firm that cannot ship products on schedule risks losing customers to faster-moving competitors.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fully remote employees report higher job satisfaction than employees who work in the office.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Departments that shifted to remote work last year experienced a decline in cross-team collaboration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The firm should not extend its remote-work pilot program to additional departments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The decline in cross-team collaboration among remote departments preceded a slowdown in the firm's product-development timeline.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A firm that cannot ship products on schedule risks losing customers to faster-moving competitors.
