questions.explanation: The conclusion is the recommendation against expanding the pilot program, C, introduced right after the concession and supported by everything that follows. A merely restates the point the author grants to remote-work advocates before arguing against expansion -- it is the concession, not the claim. B and D report the two 'because'-marked premises about the collaboration decline and its timing relative to the product slowdown; both are evidence, not the point being argued. E sits last in the stimulus and states a general risk about missed schedules, which is easy to mistake for the payoff simply because it comes at the end -- but it is a further premise explaining why the collaboration decline matters, not the author's main claim.

questions.stem:
A gym chain reports that members who use its mobile app to log workouts lose more weight, on average, than members who do not use the app. The gym's marketing director concludes that using the app causes weight loss.

The marketing director's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes that all gym members share the same weight-loss goals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that members who are already more motivated to lose weight are also more likely to use the app.

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on a sample of gym members that may be too small to be reliable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats using the app as though it were the same thing as attending the gym regularly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that the gym offers several different membership tiers.

questions.explanation: The director infers that app use causes weight loss purely from a correlation, without ruling out that motivation is a common cause of both app use and weight loss. B names exactly this failure to exclude a confounding variable, so it is correct. A raises an unrelated point about differing goals that the argument doesn't depend on. C alleges a sampling-size problem that the stimulus never raises. D wrongly conflates app use with gym attendance, a distinction the argument doesn't rely on. E is entirely irrelevant to the causal claim about weight loss.

questions.stem:
Students who take a particular art elective score higher, on average, on standardized math tests than students who do not take the elective. A researcher concludes that taking the art elective improves students' math skills.

The researcher's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: fails to consider that students who choose to take the art elective might already be stronger students overall, for reasons unrelated to the elective.

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from the results at a single school to all schools nationwide.

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that the standardized math tests accurately measure students' mathematical ability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that the art elective and the math test cover exactly the same skills.

choices.label: E
choices.text: dismisses the study's findings merely because they were funded by an arts organization.

questions.explanation: The researcher concludes that the elective improves math skills merely because elective-takers score higher, without ruling out that stronger students self-select into the elective. A states this precisely, naming the failure to exclude a preexisting-ability confound, so it is correct. B alleges an unwarranted generalization to other schools that the stimulus never makes. C challenges test validity, a point the argument's causal inference doesn't depend on. D wrongly claims the argument assumes overlapping content between the elective and the test. E accuses the argument of a funding-based dismissal that never occurs in the stimulus.

questions.stem: Principle: A city ordinance permits construction noise exceeding the standard decibel limit on residential streets only if (1) the work is an emergency repair necessary to prevent imminent harm to persons or property, and (2) the work is completed within twenty-four hours of when it began. Which of the following situations conforms to this principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A utility crew works through the night to stop an active gas leak posing imminent danger to nearby homes, but the repair is not completed until thirty hours after it began.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A contractor performs a routine kitchen renovation, unrelated to any emergency, and finishes all the noisy work within twenty hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A tree service removes a large branch that shows no signs of imminent failure, purely as a precaution, completing the job in ten hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A plumbing crew repairs a burst water main that is actively flooding a home's basement, completing the emergency repair within eighteen hours of starting.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An emergency crew repairs a retaining wall that is on the verge of collapsing onto an adjacent house, but the noisy work is spread out intermittently over three days while the crew waits between inspection phases.

questions.explanation: The principle demands both an imminent-harm emergency AND completion within twenty-four hours. D satisfies both: a flooding basement is imminent harm to property, and the repair wrapped up in eighteen hours -- this is the credited answer. A meets condition (1) (a gas leak is imminent harm) but fails condition (2): thirty hours exceeds the twenty-four-hour limit. B fails condition (1): a routine renovation is not an emergency repair, so the twenty-hour completion time is irrelevant. C fails condition (1): removing a branch with no sign of imminent failure is precautionary, not a response to imminent harm. E meets condition (1) (a collapsing wall threatens a house) but fails condition (2): the work stretches over three days, well past twenty-four hours.

questions.stem: Principle: A university's tuition-refund policy grants a full refund for a withdrawn course only if (1) the student withdraws no later than the tenth day of the term, and (2) the student submits written notice of the withdrawal to the registrar's office. Which of the following situations conforms to this principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A student decides to withdraw on the fifteenth day of the term and submits written notice to the registrar's office that same day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A student decides to withdraw on the eighth day of the term and tells her professor about the decision in person, but never contacts the registrar's office.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A student decides to withdraw on the eighth day of the term and has a friend verbally inform the registrar's front-desk staff on his behalf.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A student decides on the fifth day of the term to withdraw but does not submit written notice to the registrar's office until the twelfth day.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A student decides to withdraw on the ninth day of the term and, that same day, emails written notice of the withdrawal to the registrar's office.

questions.explanation: The principle requires both that withdrawal notice be given no later than the tenth day AND that the notice be written and directed to the registrar's office. E satisfies both: the notice was submitted on the ninth day, in writing, to the registrar -- this is the credited answer. A fails condition (1): the fifteenth day is past the tenth-day deadline, even though the notice was written and properly directed. B fails condition (2): telling a professor verbally is neither written nor sent to the registrar's office. C fails condition (2): a verbal message relayed by a friend is not written notice from the student. D fails condition (1): although the student decided to withdraw on the fifth day, the operative written notice was not submitted to the registrar until the twelfth day, past the deadline.

questions.stem: Even though newly planted trees take five to ten years to generate significant shade, the city should nonetheless expand its street-tree planting program this year rather than wait for a less expensive option. Because sidewalk temperatures in unshaded neighborhoods now regularly exceed those in shaded neighborhoods by fifteen degrees during summer heat waves, and because heat-related hospital visits are concentrated almost entirely in those unshaded neighborhoods, delaying the program would allow a known public-health hazard to continue unaddressed for years longer than necessary.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city should expand its street-tree planting program this year rather than wait for a less expensive option.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Newly planted trees take five to ten years to generate significant shade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sidewalk temperatures in unshaded neighborhoods exceed those in shaded neighborhoods by fifteen degrees during summer heat waves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heat-related hospital visits are concentrated almost entirely in unshaded neighborhoods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cheaper alternatives to the current tree-planting program are unlikely to ever become available.

questions.explanation: The conclusion sits in the first sentence, right after the concession about slow shade growth: the city should expand the program now rather than wait, which A paraphrases. B merely restates the concession the author grants before arguing anyway -- the opposite of the author's own claim. C and D report the two 'because'-marked premises about the temperature gap and hospital visits, offered as evidence for acting now, not as the claim being argued for. E overreaches: the stimulus says the city should not wait for a cheaper option this year, but it never claims cheaper options will never exist -- that stronger claim is an unsupported implication the argument does not make.

questions.stem:
Whenever a corporate board approves a merger without first holding a shareholder vote, the merger becomes subject to judicial review. TechCorp's board approved its merger with Datasoft without holding a shareholder vote. Therefore, TechCorp's shareholders are entitled to file suit to block the merger's implementation.

Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whenever a merger is subject to judicial review, its shareholders are entitled to file suit to block the merger's implementation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shareholders are entitled to file suit to block a merger's implementation only if the merger is subject to judicial review.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Datasoft's shareholders were not consulted about the merger before the board's vote.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A merger that is subject to judicial review is likely to result in shareholders filing suit to block its implementation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: TechCorp's board has approved mergers without shareholder votes on previous occasions.

questions.explanation: The premises establish, by modus ponens, that TechCorp's merger is subject to judicial review (approving without a shareholder vote triggers review, and TechCorp did exactly that). To reach the conclusion that shareholders are entitled to file suit, the argument needs a conditional guaranteeing that review status leads to suit entitlement. A supplies exactly this bridge (review → suit entitlement), making the conclusion airtight. B reverses the needed conditional (suit entitlement → review), which cannot establish that TechCorp's shareholders — already known to be under a merger subject to review — are entitled to sue; that is a classic converse error. C introduces an unestablished, irrelevant fact about consultation that never connects review status to suit entitlement. D only claims review 'likely' results in suit entitlement, a hedge that leaves open the possibility the conclusion is false, so it cannot make the argument valid. E cites TechCorp's past behavior, which has no bearing on whether this merger's review status entitles shareholders to sue now.

questions.stem:
Nutritionist: Increasing dietary fiber intake reduces the risk of heart disease. In a yearlong study, participants who raised their daily fiber intake by at least 10 grams showed significantly lower cholesterol levels at the study's end than they had at its start.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the nutritionist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fiber supplements are inexpensive and widely available in grocery stores.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many participants found it difficult to maintain a high-fiber diet after the study ended.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower cholesterol levels are strongly associated with reduced risk of heart disease.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The same participants also significantly increased their level of physical exercise during the year of the study.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fiber has been recommended by nutrition guidelines for over thirty years.

questions.explanation: The nutritionist infers that fiber intake caused lower cholesterol merely because participants who raised fiber intake also saw cholesterol drop over the same year -- a correlation treated as causation. D supplies a concurrent alternate cause: increased exercise, which independently lowers cholesterol, so the observed drop cannot be confidently attributed to fiber alone; this directly severs the premise-to-conclusion link. A discusses cost, irrelevant to whether fiber caused the change. B addresses difficulty maintaining the diet after the study, which does not undermine what happened during the study itself. C actually supports the argument's assumed link between cholesterol and heart disease rather than attacking the fiber-to-cholesterol connection. E cites longstanding recommendations, which speaks to popularity, not causal efficacy.

questions.stem:
Neighborhoods with more streetlights have lower rates of nighttime crime than neighborhoods with fewer streetlights. A city council member concludes that installing more streetlights reduces nighttime crime.

The council member's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the motives of officials who oppose the streetlight proposal rather than addressing their arguments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes that all neighborhoods have identical crime rates before any streetlights are installed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses the term "crime" to mean different things in different parts of the argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to rule out the possibility that wealthier neighborhoods fund both streetlights and other crime-reducing measures, such as private security.

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes that installing streetlights is the only way the city could reduce nighttime crime.

questions.explanation: The council member treats a correlation between streetlights and lower crime as proof of causation, without ruling out other explanations for the pattern. D supplies exactly such an alternative cause — wealth that funds both streetlights and private security — so it is correct. A alleges an ad hominem attack that is never made in the argument. B assumes a false premise about identical starting crime rates that the argument doesn't rely on. C alleges equivocation on "crime," but the term is used consistently throughout. E misstates the conclusion as an exclusivity claim, which was never asserted.

questions.stem:
Towns that built new public libraries in the past decade have seen higher rates of small-business growth than towns that did not build new libraries. A regional economist concludes that building a public library spurs small-business growth.

The economist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on business-growth figures that were self-reported by town officials.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats "small-business growth" and "economic growth" as though they were the same thing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismisses, without argument, the experience of towns that did not build libraries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that every town in the region has roughly the same population size.

choices.label: E
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that towns already growing economically for independent reasons, such as new highway access, are simply better able to fund new libraries.

questions.explanation: The economist infers that libraries spur business growth from a mere correlation, without ruling out that towns growing for independent reasons are simply better able to afford new libraries — a reverse-causation/common-cause possibility. E names this alternative cause, so it is correct. A raises a data-reliability worry that the stimulus never raises. B alleges a spurious equivocation; the argument keeps the two terms distinct. C mischaracterizes the argument as dismissing non-library towns, which it does not do. D assumes an irrelevant population-size premise that the argument doesn't require.

questions.stem: Principle: A company's remote-work policy allows an employee to work from home on a given day only if (1) the employee's manager approves the request at least twenty-four hours in advance, and (2) the employee has no client-facing meetings scheduled for that day. Which of the following situations conforms to this principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: On Wednesday morning, an employee requests to work from home the following Friday. The manager approves the request that same Wednesday, and Friday's calendar shows no client-facing meetings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An employee asks to work from home the morning of that same day, and the manager immediately approves the request. The employee has no client-facing meetings scheduled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An employee requests to work from home three days in advance and receives the manager's approval, but the employee has a client call scheduled for that afternoon.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An employee sends the manager a message forty-eight hours in advance simply announcing that she will work from home that day. The manager never responds, and the employee has no client-facing meetings scheduled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An employee requests and receives the manager's approval a week in advance for a day with no meetings on the calendar. The day before, however, a colleague adds a client-facing meeting to the employee's calendar for that day.

questions.explanation: The principle requires both manager approval given at least twenty-four hours ahead AND an empty client-facing schedule for that day. A satisfies both: approval came more than twenty-four hours before Friday, and no client meetings appear on the calendar -- this is the credited answer. B fails condition (1): approval was given the same morning, not twenty-four hours in advance. C meets condition (1) but fails condition (2): a client call is scheduled for that afternoon. D fails condition (1): announcing a plan is not the same as obtaining the manager's approval, and none was given. E met both conditions when approval was granted, but fails condition (2) as of the actual day: a client-facing meeting now appears on the calendar for that day.

questions.stem:
Every certified arborist inspects a tree before recommending its removal. No certified arborist recommends removing a tree that is still fruit-bearing. The oak on Maple Avenue is still fruit-bearing.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The oak on Maple Avenue will never be removed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any tree that is not fruit-bearing will be recommended for removal by a certified arborist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A certified arborist has already inspected the oak on Maple Avenue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No certified arborist will recommend removing the oak on Maple Avenue.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the oak on Maple Avenue stops bearing fruit, a certified arborist will recommend its removal.

questions.explanation: D is correct: the second statement is a universal claim that no certified arborist recommends removing a fruit-bearing tree, and the third statement establishes that the oak is fruit-bearing, so the conclusion follows by direct instantiation of the rule. A overreaches -- the stimulus only limits what certified arborists will recommend, not whether the tree could be removed by any other means. B treats 'fruit-bearing, therefore not recommended' as if it also meant 'not fruit-bearing, therefore recommended,' an illicit converse. C misuses the first statement: inspection is a precondition for recommending removal, but since no removal will be recommended for this tree, no inspection is required to have occurred. E again treats the fruit-bearing condition as both necessary and sufficient for a recommendation, which the stimulus never establishes.

questions.stem:
A software update may be deployed to production servers only if it has passed the automated regression suite. Version 4.2 of the billing module was deployed to production servers this morning. Therefore, version 4.2 of the billing module will not cause a customer-facing billing error this month.

Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An update that passes the automated regression suite is unlikely to cause a customer-facing billing error.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only updates that have been peer-reviewed by two engineers may be deployed to production servers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A software update does not cause a customer-facing billing error only if it has passed the automated regression suite.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Customers who report billing errors receive automatic refunds within forty-eight hours.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any software update that passes the automated regression suite will not cause a customer-facing billing error during the month it is deployed.

questions.explanation: The 'only if' rule plus the fact that version 4.2 was deployed lets us conclude, by modus ponens, that it passed the automated regression suite. To reach the conclusion that it will cause no customer-facing billing errors this month, the argument needs a conditional guaranteeing that passing the suite rules out such errors. E supplies exactly this bridge (passed suite → no billing errors), making the conclusion airtight. A only claims such errors are 'unlikely,' a hedge that leaves room for the conclusion to be false. B introduces an unrelated deployment requirement (peer review) that never connects passing the suite to the absence of billing errors. C reverses the needed relationship (no billing errors → passed the suite), a converse error that cannot establish this update will avoid errors. D's fact about refund policy has no bearing on whether the update itself causes billing errors.

questions.stem:
A pesticide may be approved for agricultural use only if it has undergone a decade-long toxicity study. This year, the Agriculture Ministry approved the pesticide Zorvex for agricultural use. Therefore, Zorvex will not accumulate in groundwater supplies near farmland where it is applied.

Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A pesticide that has undergone a decade-long toxicity study is somewhat less likely to accumulate in groundwater supplies near treated farmland.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any pesticide that has undergone a decade-long toxicity study will not accumulate in groundwater supplies near farmland where it is applied.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A pesticide does not accumulate in groundwater supplies near treated farmland only if it has undergone a decade-long toxicity study.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Farmers who apply Zorvex to their fields must wear protective equipment during application.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zorvex has already been approved for agricultural use in several neighboring countries.

questions.explanation: Because approval requires the decade-long toxicity study, and Zorvex was approved this year, modus ponens establishes that it underwent the study. The conclusion — that Zorvex will not accumulate in groundwater near treated farmland — requires a further conditional linking the study to that outcome. B supplies exactly this bridge (underwent study → no groundwater accumulation), guaranteeing the conclusion. A only claims accumulation is 'somewhat less likely,' a hedge that cannot rule out accumulation. C reverses the needed relationship (no accumulation → underwent study), a converse error that cannot show this already-studied pesticide will not accumulate. D introduces an unrelated safety requirement (protective equipment) that never connects the study to groundwater outcomes. E's fact about foreign approvals has no bearing on whether Zorvex accumulates in groundwater near farmland where it is applied.

questions.stem:
Nutritionist: Last year, Acme Corp replaced its cafeteria's standard menu with nutritionist-designed, low-sugar meals. This year, the number of employee sick days taken company-wide fell by 18 percent compared to last year. The new menu must be responsible for the drop in sick days.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the nutritionist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cafeteria's new menu costs the company more per meal than the old menu did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The composition of Acme's workforce — age, department, and health history — was nearly identical in the two years compared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several employees said they enjoy the taste of the new menu more than the old one.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A well-known nutrition expert has publicly praised menus similar to Acme's new one.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The same year the menu changed, Acme also let employees with minor illnesses work from home instead of taking a sick day.

questions.explanation: The argument infers that the menu caused fewer sick days from a mere before-and-after correlation. B strengthens it by ruling out a key alternative explanation: that the drop reflects a change in who makes up the workforce (e.g., a shift toward employees already less prone to illness) rather than any effect of the menu. With the population held constant, the menu becomes the more plausible cause. A raises cost, which bears on expense, not on whether the menu improved health. C shows enjoyment of taste, which says nothing about whether health, and thus sick days, actually improved. D is an appeal to authority — an expert's praise doesn't show the menu caused this particular drop. E actually undermines the argument: if mildly ill employees now work from home instead of calling in sick, the metric could fall for administrative reasons unrelated to any real health improvement, so E is a weakener, not a strengthener.

questions.stem:
School administrator: Since our district adopted the Read-25 program, which requires all elementary students to read silently for 25 minutes each morning, districtwide standardized reading scores have risen by 12 percent over the past two years. The Read-25 program must be responsible for this improvement.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the administrator's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Read-25 program cost the district less to implement than administrators had originally budgeted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prominent education researcher has publicly praised programs similar to Read-25.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reading scores in neighboring districts that did not adopt Read-25 remained flat over the same two years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The standardized reading test given this year was calibrated to be somewhat easier than the version given two years ago.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many parents have reported that their children enjoy the daily reading time.

questions.explanation: The administrator infers causation from a two-year rise in scores that coincided with adopting Read-25. C strengthens the inference by supplying an implicit control group: comparable districts that did not adopt the program saw no such rise, which rules out a shared external cause — such as a statewide curriculum shift or a general trend — and isolates Read-25 as the likely factor. A speaks to budget, not to whether the program raised scores. B is an appeal to authority: praise for similar programs doesn't establish that Read-25 caused this district's gain. D actually weakens the argument, since an easier test could account for higher scores with no real improvement in reading ability. E reports satisfaction, not achievement, and so is irrelevant to whether scores rose because of the program.

questions.stem:
Public safety official: Since the city installed brighter LED streetlights along Main Avenue last year, nighttime pedestrian accidents on that stretch have dropped by 30 percent. The brighter lighting must be responsible for the decline.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the official's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Traffic volume and posted speed limits along Main Avenue have not changed since the new lights were installed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The new LED streetlights consume less electricity than the sodium-vapor lights they replaced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A city council member with an engineering background voted in favor of the lighting upgrade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city also lowered the speed limit on Main Avenue by 10 miles per hour when the new lights were installed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The city plans to install similar LED lighting in three other neighborhoods next year.

questions.explanation: The official attributes a drop in accidents to the new lighting based on a before-and-after comparison. A strengthens this by ruling out the two most obvious alternative causes of fewer accidents — reduced traffic and lower speed limits — leaving the lighting change as the more likely explanation for the decline. B addresses energy efficiency, which has no bearing on accident rates. C is an appeal to authority: a council member's engineering background doesn't show the lighting caused the drop. D actually weakens the argument by introducing exactly the kind of confound A rules out — a lowered speed limit that could itself explain fewer accidents. E concerns future plans elsewhere and says nothing about what caused the change already observed on Main Avenue.

questions.stem:
Store manager: Our flagship store switched to new self-checkout software last spring, and average checkout wait times at that store fell by 40 percent over the following six months. Clearly, installing the new software caused the drop in wait times.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the manager's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The self-checkout software received a favorable review in a widely read technology trade magazine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The store also hired six additional cashiers to staff traditional checkout lanes during the same six-month period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Customers who used the new self-checkout kiosks reported that they were easy to operate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Installing the new software cost the store more than the previous checkout system had.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The store's total daily customer volume increased by 15 percent over the same six months.

questions.explanation: The manager attributes the drop in wait times solely to the new software based on the timing of the installation coinciding with the improvement. B supplies a concurrent alternate cause -- additional cashier staffing -- that could account for shorter average wait times independent of the software, undermining the causal claim. A cites a magazine review, which speaks to reputation, not to what actually caused wait times to fall. C reports user satisfaction with ease of use, which does not establish that the software rather than something else reduced overall wait times. D raises installation cost, an irrelevant consideration. E, if anything, makes the software's apparent effect more impressive since wait times fell despite more customers, so it does not weaken and may even bolster the conclusion.

questions.stem:
Orchard owner: We introduced ladybugs into the orchard to control the aphid population. Aphid counts, which had been rising for months, fell sharply within three weeks of the release. Clearly, introducing the ladybugs caused the decline in aphids.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the orchard owner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The three-week period in which aphid counts fell coincided with an unusually cold snap known to sharply reduce aphid reproduction rates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ladybugs are commonly used by orchard owners across the region to manage pest populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Purchasing and releasing the ladybugs cost the orchard less than a comparable application of pesticide would have.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aphids are a significant threat to fruit tree yields if left unchecked.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some of the released ladybugs migrated to a neighboring farm within a month of the release.

questions.explanation: The owner infers that releasing ladybugs caused the aphid decline merely because the decline followed the release -- a temporal correlation, not proof of causation. A supplies a concurrent alternate cause: an unusually cold period known to independently suppress aphid reproduction, which could fully explain the drop without any effect from the ladybugs, undermining the causal claim. B cites the popularity of the ladybug method elsewhere, irrelevant to what happened in this orchard. C addresses cost, not causation. D restates why aphid control matters generally, not why the ladybugs specifically caused this decline. E's detail about later migration does not address what caused the decline that had already occurred within the first three weeks.

questions.stem:
Public health official: Since our city began requiring restaurants to post calorie counts on menus five years ago, the citywide obesity rate has fallen by three percentage points. Clearly, then, mandatory calorie labeling has caused the decline in the obesity rate.

The public health official's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: presupposes what it sets out to prove.

choices.label: B
choices.text: takes for granted that no factor other than calorie labeling could account for the decline in the obesity rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the whole city from evidence concerning only a few restaurants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient to reduce obesity as though it were also necessary to reduce it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects the effectiveness of calorie labeling merely because some restaurants have not complied with it.

questions.explanation: The official infers causation from mere temporal correlation: the labeling requirement preceded the decline, so it is credited as the cause, without ruling out other explanations (broader health campaigns, economic shifts, changing food trends). That is exactly what B names. A is wrong because the argument never assumes its conclusion as a premise; it offers a flawed causal inference, not circular reasoning. C is wrong because the argument cites a citywide statistic, not a restaurant subsample, so there is no part-to-whole generalization. D is wrong because the argument never claims labeling is required for obesity to decline; it claims labeling caused the decline, which is a different error. E is wrong because the passage never discusses noncompliance or rejects anything on that basis.

questions.stem:
Librarian: This year, mystery novels were checked out more times than books from any other single genre in our collection. Clearly, mystery is our patrons' favorite genre. Since a public library's acquisitions budget should track what its patrons love most, the mystery collection should receive the largest share of next year's acquisitions budget.

The librarian's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on checkout data from a single year to draw a conclusion about patrons' preferences over time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: equates the frequency with which mystery novels are checked out with how highly patrons regard the mystery genre relative to others, though frequent checkouts may simply reflect that mystery novels are quick reads that get returned and reborrowed often.

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes, without justification, that patrons who check out mystery novels never also check out books from other genres.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats a proposed budget policy as though it had already been adopted and implemented.

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that some patrons acquire mystery novels by purchasing them rather than borrowing them from the library.

questions.explanation: The librarian moves from checkout frequency (how often mystery novels leave the shelves) to patron preference (how much patrons value the genre above others), treating the two as the same thing. A genre can top the checkout count simply because its books are short and get returned and reborrowed quickly, not because patrons prize it most; B names this shift. A alleges a hasty generalization from one year of data, but the conclusion concerns next year's budget given this year's demonstrated demand, not a claim about long-term preference stability, so A misdescribes the argument. C invents an unstated and irrelevant assumption about exclusive borrowing habits that the argument never needs. D is inapplicable because the librarian only recommends a budget allocation and never treats it as already enacted. E raises purchasing habits, a consideration outside the scope of an argument built entirely on library checkout data.

questions.stem:
Urban planner: The city council's new zoning law requires that fifteen percent of units in any large residential development be designated "affordable housing." Developers have complied by pricing those units at just below the citywide median sale price. Because compliance with the law has been high, the zoning law is succeeding at making housing affordable for low-income residents.

The urban planner's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes that every developer subject to the zoning law has complied with it in good faith.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a correlation between the zoning law's passage and current housing prices as evidence that the law caused those prices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the citywide housing market from the pricing practices of only a few developments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: equates housing priced just below the citywide median sale price with housing that is genuinely within reach of low-income residents, even though the median sale price may still be far higher than what such residents can afford.

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that low-income residents prefer to live in large residential developments rather than in smaller buildings.

questions.explanation: The planner treats "affordable housing" in its technical, regulatory sense (priced just below the citywide median) as equivalent to housing that is actually affordable for low-income residents, though a price just under the citywide median can still be well beyond a low-income budget. D names this shift. A is inapplicable because compliance is stated as a given fact, not an assumption the argument needs to be true in good faith. B is wrong because the argument never claims the law caused housing prices generally, only that compliant units were priced a certain way. C mischaracterizes the premise, which describes developers broadly, not "only a few" developments. E is irrelevant: preferences about building size have no bearing on whether the mandated units are financially reachable.

questions.stem: In Meadowbrook County, farmers planted a record-high proportion of a new drought-resistant corn hybrid this year—a hybrid documented to outyield standard corn under moderately dry conditions. Yet the county's total corn yield this year was lower than last year's, when farmers planted almost none of the new hybrid. Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: This year's growing season brought rainfall levels far below normal—well beyond the moderate dryness the hybrid was bred to tolerate—so the hybrid's yield advantage was overwhelmed by the severity of the drought.

choices.label: B
choices.text: National corn prices fell by double digits this year compared to last year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The record planting of the drought-resistant hybrid was concentrated on the county's largest farms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drought-resistant hybrid tends to produce its highest yields specifically in years of severe, rather than moderate, drought.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Last year's corn crop, but not this year's, was afflicted by a fungal blight that has since been eradicated.

questions.explanation: The paradox: record planting of a hybrid known to outyield standard corn under dry conditions, yet total yield fell. (A) resolves it by showing the hybrid's documented advantage applies only to moderate dryness—this year's drought exceeded that threshold, so even the superior hybrid could not prevent an overall decline; both facts hold simultaneously. (B) is out of scope: price movements don't explain yield. (C) only describes where planting occurred, not why total yield fell; it doesn't address the discrepancy. (D) deepens the paradox—if severe drought is exactly when the hybrid performs best, the yield drop becomes even harder to explain. (E) also deepens the paradox: removing a disease that suppressed last year's yield should have made this year's yield relatively higher, not lower, making the actual decline more puzzling, not less.

questions.stem: In Silverwood National Park, the gray wolf population has more than doubled over the past decade due to a successful reintroduction program. Yet the population of elk, the wolves' primary prey, has not declined over that same period—it has remained essentially stable. Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The park's wolves hunt in coordinated packs, which increases their hunting success rate compared to solitary wolves.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Silverwood's wolves prey primarily on elk that are old, sick, or injured—individuals that generally would not have survived long or reproduced successfully regardless, so increased predation has mainly removed elk that contributed little to future population growth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elk are herbivores that feed primarily on the grasses and shrubs found throughout the park's meadows.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A separate elk population in a neighboring, wolf-free preserve has grown substantially over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reintroduction program initially released only a small number of breeding pairs of wolves a decade ago.

questions.explanation: The paradox: the wolf population more than doubled, yet elk numbers held steady. (B) resolves it by showing predation has concentrated on elk unlikely to have added to the population anyway, so the rise in wolf numbers hasn't translated into a corresponding loss of reproductively significant elk—both facts can be true together. (A) deepens the paradox: a higher hunting success rate should mean more elk killed and a declining population, making the observed stability harder to explain. (C) is out of scope: elk diet says nothing about predation's effect on their population. (D) is out of scope: a wolf-free preserve is a separate population and cannot explain trends within Silverwood itself. (E) explains only how the wolf population grew from a small founding group, not why elk numbers failed to fall in response.

questions.stem:
City council member: Two years ago, Midvale launched a curbside composting program, and the city's landfill waste dropped by 30 percent within a year. Because Elmwood resembles Midvale in population size and household density, launching a curbside composting program in Elmwood will likewise reduce its landfill waste by about 30 percent.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the council member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Composting bins are inexpensive to manufacture and distribute.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Midvale residents widely praised the composting program in a satisfaction survey.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elmwood's landfill waste has increased slightly over the past several years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other cities besides Midvale have also successfully reduced landfill waste through composting programs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unlike Midvale, Elmwood does not have municipal trucks equipped to separately collect compostable waste, and outfitting them would take several years.

questions.explanation: The council member reasons by analogy: because Elmwood resembles Midvale in population and density, a composting program should produce a similar result there. E identifies a relevant disanalogy -- Elmwood lacks the collection infrastructure that made Midvale's program work and cannot quickly acquire it -- which severs the inference that demographic similarity implies similarity in outcome. A and B raise cost and popularity in Midvale, neither of which bears on whether Elmwood's program would succeed. C's preexisting waste trend in Elmwood does not address the comparison to Midvale's causal result one way or the other. D actually adds more supporting analogues rather than weakening the argument. Only E attacks the premise-to-conclusion link directly.

questions.stem:
Analyst: After installing new machinery last year, our factory used twelve percent less energy to produce the same volume of goods as the year before. Since efficiency is simply a matter of using fewer resources to achieve the same output, the new machinery made the factory more efficient. It follows that operating the factory cost less last year than it did the year before.

The analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers that the decrease in energy use was caused by the new machinery, without ruling out that the factory simply produced a smaller volume of goods last year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a twelve percent decrease in energy use as though it were a decrease of twelve absolute units of energy, rather than a percentage of a larger total.

choices.label: C
choices.text: concludes that the factory's overall profits increased without providing any data about the factory's revenue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the factory's future operating costs based on a single year of data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: equates using fewer resources to produce a given output with spending less money to operate the factory, even though resource efficiency and total operating cost can diverge because of factors such as energy prices, maintenance, and labor.

questions.explanation: The analyst equates technical efficiency (fewer resources per unit of output) with financial cost (money spent to operate the factory), but these can diverge: energy prices, maintenance needs, or labor costs could rise even as resource efficiency improves. E names this measure shift. A is contradicted by the stimulus, which states output volume held constant, so the alternative it proposes cannot explain the data. B alleges a numerical misreading the analyst never makes; the argument treats the percentage correctly as a proportional decrease. C is out of scope because the analyst concludes only that operating cost fell, never mentioning profit or revenue. D mischaracterizes the conclusion, which is a claim about last year's cost compared to the prior year, not a prediction about future years.

questions.stem: After a hospital introduced a new hand-hygiene training program, the proportion of staff observed washing their hands according to protocol rose from 62 percent to 91 percent. Yet the hospital's overall rate of hospital-acquired infections was no lower in the year after the program than in the year before. Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The hospital's patient satisfaction survey scores improved after the training program was introduced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Studies of similar programs at other hospitals have found that compliance rates typically decline within a year unless reinforced by ongoing training.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nurses who attended the training reported that they found the hand-washing techniques easy to remember and apply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hospital also introduced a new antibiotic protocol during the same year, one shown at other facilities to reduce post-procedure infection rates by roughly 30 percent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: During that year, the hospital began admitting significantly more patients transferred from a nearby long-term-care facility that closed, and these patients had unusually weakened immune systems that made them more susceptible to infection independent of hand hygiene.

questions.explanation: The paradox: measured hand-hygiene compliance rose dramatically, yet the infection rate didn't budge. (E) resolves it by identifying a shift in the patient population toward individuals far more vulnerable to infection for reasons unrelated to hygiene—so improved hand-washing could be genuinely reducing hygiene-related transmission while a sicker patient mix pushed the overall rate back up, letting both facts hold. (A) is out of scope: satisfaction scores don't bear on infection rates. (B) is a generalization about other hospitals' future compliance trends, not a fact about what actually happened at this hospital during the year in question, so it doesn't address the current discrepancy. (C) explains only why compliance rose (staff found the training memorable), saying nothing about the infection rate. (D) deepens the paradox: an additional intervention independently expected to lower infections should have made the flat rate even more surprising, not less.

questions.stem:
Marine biologists agree that a coral reef's ability to survive a period of unusually warm ocean water depends heavily on the reef's genetic diversity: greater diversity gives a reef's coral colonies more chances of carrying heat-tolerant gene variants. Of all the reefs in the Coral Strait region, Kestrel Reef has the greatest genetic diversity. Marine biologists therefore predict that, of the region's reefs, Kestrel Reef is the one most likely to survive the coming period of unusually warm water.

Which one of the following is an assumption required by the marine biologists' prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Kestrel Reef's genetic diversity arose primarily through natural processes rather than human intervention.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genetic diversity is the only factor that affects a coral reef's ability to survive warm water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kestrel Reef will receive priority protection from regional conservation authorities because of its genetic diversity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No other reef in the Coral Strait region has some other advantage relevant to surviving warm water great enough to offset Kestrel Reef's lead in genetic diversity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every coral colony within Kestrel Reef carries at least one heat-tolerant gene variant.

questions.explanation: The prediction moves from 'Kestrel has the most genetic diversity' to 'Kestrel is most likely to survive,' which only follows if nothing else could tip the balance toward a different reef. D supplies exactly that: negate it - suppose some other reef DOES have an offsetting advantage - and Kestrel's diversity lead no longer makes it the likeliest survivor, so the prediction fails; D is required. A is out of scope: how the diversity arose doesn't bear on survival odds. B overshoots what's needed - the argument only requires that no other factor overcome Kestrel's edge, not that diversity is the sole relevant factor, so B is stronger than necessary. C is irrelevant: conservation funding doesn't affect biological survival likelihood. E misreads the premise, which says diversity gives 'more chances that some colonies' carry heat-tolerant genes, not that every colony does; E is an unwarranted overstatement the argument never needs.

questions.stem:
Swim coach: Since our team started reviewing weekly underwater video of each athlete's stroke technique, athletes' race times have improved by an average of 3 percent this season. The video review sessions must be responsible for the improvement.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the coach's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The underwater cameras used for video review were relatively inexpensive compared to other training equipment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An Olympic swimming coach has recommended video review as a training tool.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The team also hired a new strength-and-conditioning coach at the start of this season.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Athletes who received the most correction feedback during video sessions improved their times the most, while athletes who received little feedback improved the least.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several athletes said that watching themselves swim on video was initially embarrassing.

questions.explanation: The coach infers that video review caused the season's improvement from a general correlation between the new practice and faster times. D strengthens the argument by confirming the underlying mechanism: within the team, the amount of feedback an athlete received tracks the size of that athlete's improvement, a dose-response pattern that is hard to explain unless the video review itself is driving the gains. A concerns cost, not effectiveness. B is an appeal to authority — a coach's endorsement doesn't demonstrate that video review caused this team's improvement. C actually weakens the argument by introducing a rival explanation, the new strength-and-conditioning coach, for the same improvement. E describes athletes' discomfort, which is irrelevant to whether the sessions improved performance.

questions.stem:
Manager: To qualify for the senior analyst role at our firm, an employee must complete the advanced certification course. Priya has completed the advanced certification course. So Priya will be promoted to senior analyst.

The manager's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers that Priya lacks any additional qualifications, since none were mentioned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats the fact that the course does not guarantee promotion as proof that the course is irrelevant to promotion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a single employee's situation to a conclusion about every employee at the firm.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats a condition required for the promotion as though it were, by itself, enough to secure the promotion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that the certification requirement has changed since Priya completed the course.

questions.explanation: The stated rule makes completing the course a necessary condition for promotion, not a sufficient one. From the fact that Priya satisfied that necessary condition, the manager concludes she will be promoted, illegitimately treating the requirement as though meeting it alone guarantees the outcome. That is D. A is wrong: the argument never addresses (nor denies) Priya's other qualifications, so this criticism has no textual basis. B is wrong: the manager never claims the course is worthless or irrelevant; that is the reverse of the actual error. C is wrong: the conclusion concerns only Priya, not a firm-wide claim about every employee. E is wrong: nothing in the passage suggests the requirement changed; this introduces an unsupported possibility.

questions.stem:
Coach: This season, our team's average points scored per game increased by ten points over last season's average. Our team's performance has therefore improved this season. Since a team is nothing more than the sum of its individual players, every player on this year's roster must have improved compared to last season.

The coach's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats an increase in the team's aggregate scoring average as proof that each individual player's performance improved, without ruling out that the increase could instead result from personnel changes or a shift in playing time among returning players.

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that points scored per game is the only meaningful measure of a player's contribution to the team.

choices.label: C
choices.text: predicts that the team's scoring average will continue to rise in future seasons based on a single season's improvement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: dismisses evidence against the coach's conclusion by appealing to the players' popularity rather than to their statistics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that some opposing teams may have also increased their scoring averages this season.

questions.explanation: "Improved" shifts from a team-level, aggregate sense (the average went up) to a distributive, individual sense (every single player got better), as if a team's total were nothing but a simple sum of unchanged parts. But the aggregate could rise because of new players, cut players, or redistributed playing time, with no single returning player improving at all; A names exactly this scope shift. B alleges an unstated assumption about points being the sole measure of contribution, which the coach's argument does not require. C mischaracterizes the conclusion, which is about last season versus this season, not future seasons. D is inapplicable since nothing in the passage appeals to popularity. E raises other teams' performance, which is irrelevant to whether this team's own players individually improved.

questions.stem:
Every accredited clinic is inspected each year. Every clinic that is inspected each year keeps a public compliance log. Riverside is an accredited clinic. Therefore, Riverside keeps a public compliance log.

The pattern of reasoning above is most closely paralleled by which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most novels that win the prize are translated into English, and most translated novels sell well abroad. This novel won the prize, so it sells well abroad.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every bonded courier is fingerprinted, and every fingerprinted courier is assigned an ID number. Lopez has an ID number, so Lopez is a bonded courier.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every commissioned mural is catalogued, and every catalogued artwork is insured. The atrium piece is a commissioned mural, so the atrium piece is insured.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every scholarship recipient volunteers, and everyone who volunteers earns service credit. Nina is not a scholarship recipient, so Nina earns no service credit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every registered drone is logged, and every logged drone is either taxed or exempted. This drone is registered, so it is taxed.

questions.explanation: The stimulus chains two universals and instantiates: all P are Q; all Q are R; a is P; therefore a is R. C reproduces it exactly (mural to catalogued to insured, and the atrium piece is a mural, so it is insured). A downgrades both universals to 'most,' so the probabilistic links cannot chain to a certainty about a particular novel. B runs the chain backward, inferring membership from the end term (ID number)—affirming the consequent. D denies the antecedent, concluding from 'not P' that the consequent fails. E replaces the second universal's predicate with a disjunction (taxed or exempted), so 'taxed' cannot be guaranteed. Only C preserves both the validity and the forward P-to-R structure.

questions.stem:
If a bill has broad support, it clears committee. If a bill clears committee, it reaches the floor for a vote. The reform bill never reached the floor for a vote. Therefore, the reform bill did not have broad support.

Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a resume is flagged, it goes to a recruiter. If it goes to a recruiter, it gets a phone screen. This resume got a phone screen, so it was flagged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the river floods, the trail closes. If the trail closes, the race is postponed. The river did not flood, so the race was not postponed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a shrub is native, it needs little watering. Most shrubs that need little watering survive the summer. This shrub did not survive the summer, so it is not native.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a nominee is endorsed, she secures funding. If she gains media coverage, she wins her primary. She did not win her primary, so she was not endorsed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the alarm is armed, the sensors are live. If the sensors are live, the log records any motion. The log recorded no motion overnight. So the alarm was not armed.

questions.explanation: The stimulus chains two conditionals and applies modus tollens: P to Q; Q to R; not R; therefore not P. E reproduces it—armed to sensors live to log records motion; the log recorded none; so it was not armed. A affirms the consequent, inferring the antecedent (flagged) from the final result (phone screen). B denies the antecedent, moving from 'river did not flood' to 'race not postponed.' C downgrades the second link to 'most,' so the chain cannot deliver a valid contrapositive from 'did not survive.' D breaks the chain: the middle terms (secures funding vs. gains media coverage) do not connect, so 'not endorsed' does not follow from 'did not win.' Only E preserves the valid P-Q-R-then-deny-R form.

questions.stem:
Analyst: If a company's quarterly earnings beat analyst forecasts, its share price rises the next trading day. Meridian Corp's share price rose the trading day after it released its quarterly report. It follows that Meridian's earnings beat the forecasts.

Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its flawed reasoning to the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a highway is salted before a storm, it stays free of ice. The county salted Route 9 before Tuesday's storm, so Route 9 stayed free of ice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a patient has completed the antibiotic course, the follow-up culture shows no bacterial growth. Ms. Alvarez's culture showed no growth, so she completed the course.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a seedling receives direct sun, it flowers early. This seedling gets no direct sun, so it will not flower early.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the smoke alarm is working, it sounds when the test button is held. The alarm did not sound when the button was held, so it is not working.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every tenant who pays rent late is sent a notice. Mr. Okafor paid his rent late this month, so he was sent a notice.

questions.explanation: The analyst reasons: earnings-beat -> price rise; the price rose; therefore earnings beat. That affirms the consequent, since a price rise could have other causes. (B) matches exactly: completed course -> no growth; no growth observed; therefore completed course. (A) is a valid modus ponens (salted, so ice-free). (C) denies the antecedent (no sun, so no early flowering) -- invalid, but a different conditional error. (D) is a valid modus tollens (didn't sound, so not working). (E) is a valid universal instantiation (paid late, so sent a notice). Only (B) commits the analyst's affirm-the-consequent flaw.

questions.stem:
Harbormaster: If the evening ferry is running, the harbor cafe stays open past nine. Tonight the evening ferry is not running. So the harbor cafe will not stay open past nine.

Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its flawed reasoning to the harbormaster's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a bill has bipartisan backing, it clears the committee. The transit bill cleared the committee, so it had bipartisan backing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the vaccine is effective, reported cases decline. Reported cases did not decline, so the vaccine is not effective.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a student submits the essay before Friday, she is entered in the prize draw. Devon did not submit his essay before Friday, so Devon is not entered in the draw.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the thermostat is set below sixty, the heater runs. The thermostat is set below sixty, so the heater is running.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every club member who renewed by June received a badge. Priya renewed by June, so Priya received a badge.

questions.explanation: The harbormaster reasons: ferry running -> cafe open late; ferry not running; therefore cafe not open late. That denies the antecedent, since the cafe could stay open for other reasons. (C) matches: submits early -> entered; Devon didn't submit early; therefore not entered. (A) affirms the consequent (cleared committee, so bipartisan) -- invalid, but the opposite conditional error. (B) is a valid modus tollens (cases didn't decline, so not effective). (D) is a valid modus ponens (set below sixty, so running). (E) is a valid universal instantiation (renewed, so got a badge). Only (C) commits the deny-the-antecedent flaw.

questions.stem: Over the past five years, ridership on Ridgeline Transit's commuter rail line grew by 40 percent. Yet automobile traffic congestion on the parallel highway during rush hour did not decrease at all over that same period. Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve this apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ridgeline Transit added several new rail cars during the five years to accommodate its growing ridership.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rail line's ticket prices rose by 15 percent over the five years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The region's total commuter population grew by more than 60 percent over the same five years, so despite the rail line's growth, the number of commuters choosing to drive also increased substantially.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The parallel highway gained two additional lanes of capacity through a widening project completed during the five years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ridgeline Transit's on-time performance improved significantly over the five years.

questions.explanation: The paradox: rail ridership rose sharply, yet highway congestion didn't ease at all. (C) resolves it: if the overall pool of commuters grew even faster than rail ridership, the rail line could be absorbing real new demand while the number of drivers still rose, holding congestion steady. (A) explains only how the transit agency accommodated more riders—it says nothing about why driving volume held up, so it addresses only one side of the paradox. (B) is out of scope: fare changes don't bear on congestion levels. (D) deepens the paradox: added highway capacity plus rising rail ridership should have eased congestion further, making its absence more surprising, not less. (E) is out of scope: better on-time performance might explain why riders chose the train, but it does not explain why car traffic failed to drop.

questions.stem:
A city planner claims: "Every proposed park design that includes a water feature will exceed our maintenance budget, so we should reject any design with a water feature." A colleague responds: "That's not quite right. The Riverside plan includes a decorative fountain, yet its projected upkeep cost is the lowest of all twelve submitted designs — well under budget."

The colleague responds to the city planner's claim by

choices.label: A
choices.text: presenting a specific case that meets the stated condition but not the predicted outcome, thereby refuting the planner's generalization with a counterexample

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogous conclusion about a different budgeting decision and arguing that the same reasoning must apply there as well

choices.label: C
choices.text: showing that accepting the planner's claim would lead to a result that is self-contradictory or plainly absurd

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing the judgment of a budget expert whose credentials make that expert's opinion authoritative on the matter

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that the only two explanations for the fountain's low cost are the planner's assumption and mere coincidence, then eliminating coincidence

questions.explanation: A is correct: the colleague identifies a case — the Riverside plan — that satisfies the planner's stated condition (includes a water feature) but not the predicted consequence (exceeding budget), which is precisely how a counterexample refutes a universal generalization. B is wrong because the colleague never reasons by analogy to a different budgeting decision; the response stays within the same set of designs. C is wrong because the colleague never claims the planner's view produces an absurd or self-contradictory result — only that it produces a false prediction. D is wrong because no expert's authority is invoked; the evidence offered is the Riverside plan's own projected costs, not anyone's opinion. E is wrong because the colleague does not present or eliminate rival explanations for the fountain's low cost; the point is simply that the planner's generalization has an exception.

questions.stem:
A software company can win a lucrative government contract only if its product passes an independent security audit. The company's product has just passed an independent security audit conducted by GlobalCert, a security firm with an excellent reputation. The company's chief executive therefore announced that the company will win the government contract.

The chief executive's conclusion depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: GlobalCert's security audits are more rigorous than those conducted by other security-auditing firms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No requirement other than passing a security audit could prevent the company from winning the government contract.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The company has previously won government contracts on the strength of a security audit alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a company's product fails an independent security audit, the government will not award that company the contract.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The government awards this particular contract to only one company each year.

questions.explanation: Passing the audit is stated only as a necessary condition for winning ('can win only if'), so from 'passed the audit' alone nothing follows about actually winning unless nothing else stands in the way. B supplies that missing link; negate it - suppose some other requirement could still block the win - and the CEO's conclusion no longer follows, so B is required. A is out of scope: relative audit rigor doesn't establish that passing guarantees the contract. C is irrelevant history that doesn't bear on this contract. D merely restates the given 'only if' premise in its contrapositive form (failing the audit blocks the contract); it's already true given the premises and adds nothing to bridge from 'passed' to 'will win,' so it isn't the missing assumption. E introduces an unstated, unnecessary detail about how many companies are awarded the contract.

questions.stem:
Community organizer: A sustainable neighborhood is one that can meet its own needs without depleting resources for future generations. Our neighborhood has sustained a stable population and tax base for over twenty years. Therefore, our neighborhood is a sustainable neighborhood.

The community organizer's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes that a neighborhood's needs never change over a twenty-year period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers that because the neighborhood has been stable for twenty years, it will remain stable indefinitely.

choices.label: C
choices.text: trades on two different senses of "sustain," shifting from a neighborhood's staying stable over time to a neighborhood's not depleting resources for the future.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the absence of any reported resource shortages as proof that the neighborhood does not deplete resources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: concludes that the neighborhood meets the stated definition merely because community members believe that it does.

questions.explanation: The definition given uses "sustainable" to mean not depleting resources for the future, but the evidence offered concerns a different sense of the word: a stable population and tax base sustained over time. The argument treats satisfying this second, unrelated sense as though it satisfied the first, which is equivocation, named by C. A is wrong: the argument never claims needs are static; that issue is not raised. B is wrong: the conclusion is about the present, not a prediction of indefinite future stability. D is wrong: no resource shortages or reports are mentioned anywhere in the passage. E is wrong: the argument cites financial and demographic stability, not community members' beliefs, as its evidence.

questions.stem:
Board member: The gallery's loss last quarter was caused either by falling attendance or by rising rent. Attendance did fall last quarter. So rising rent was not a factor in the loss.

Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its flawed reasoning to the board member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The malfunction is in either the software or the hardware. Testing shows it is not in the software. So it is in the hardware.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proposal is not both cheap and fast. It is certainly cheap. So it is not fast.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the gallery had cut its staff, its costs would have dropped. Its costs did drop. So the gallery cut its staff.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marcus was late this morning because he either overslept or missed his train. He did oversleep. So he did not miss his train.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the loss came from rent, then rent rose this quarter. Rent did not rise. So the loss did not come from rent.

questions.explanation: The board member treats an 'either/or' as exclusive: the loss came from falling attendance or rising rent; attendance fell; therefore rent was not a factor. But both causes could operate at once, so affirming one disjunct does not rule out the other. (D) commits the same error: overslept or missed the train; he overslept; so he didn't miss the train. (A) is a valid disjunctive syllogism (not software, so hardware). (B) is a valid De Morgan inference (not both cheap and fast; cheap; so not fast). (C) affirms the consequent (cut staff -> costs drop; costs dropped; so cut staff). (E) is a valid modus tollens (rent didn't rise, so the loss was not from rent). Only (D) affirms a disjunct.

questions.stem:
An engineer argues: "Last month, the factory's defect rate fell sharply. Either the new quality-control checklist caused the drop, the milder weather reduced humidity-related warping, or the reassignment of the night-shift supervisor improved oversight. We can rule out the weather: temperature and humidity logs show conditions nearly identical to the prior month. We can also rule out the supervisor reassignment: the new supervisor wasn't scheduled to start until three weeks after the drop had already leveled off. So the checklist must be responsible."

The engineer's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: inferring that the checklist caused the drop merely because the two events happened to occur around the same time, without considering whether other factors might explain the timing

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing a general rule about defect rates from a single factory's experience and applying that rule to the manufacturing industry as a whole

choices.label: C
choices.text: presuming, without independent proof, that quality-control checklists are inherently effective, and using that presumption to account for the data

choices.label: D
choices.text: eliminating two competing explanations for the observed drop by citing independent evidence against each, leaving the remaining explanation as the best-supported one

choices.label: E
choices.text: comparing the factory's situation to an analogous case at a different plant where a checklist also coincided with a reduction in defects

questions.explanation: D is correct: the engineer considers three candidate explanations, rules out two of them using independent evidence (matching weather logs; a supervisor start date after the drop had leveled off), and concludes that the surviving explanation is responsible — the classic method of eliminating alternatives. A is wrong because the engineer does not rely on mere timing; the argument explicitly rules out the two other candidates using evidence unrelated to timing, rather than inferring causation from correlation alone. B is wrong because no general industry-wide rule is drawn or applied; the conclusion is limited to this factory's defect rate. C is wrong because the engineer never simply presumes checklists work; the conclusion rests on ruling out rivals, not on an unproven assumption about checklists in general. E is wrong because no other plant or analogous case is mentioned anywhere in the argument.

questions.stem:
Historians know that a town's founding date is best established by contemporaneous written records. The earliest surviving municipal document that mentions the town of Millbrook is dated 1841, and no surviving document assigns Millbrook an earlier founding date. Historians have therefore concluded that Millbrook was founded in 1841.

Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historians' reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Millbrook's 1841 municipal document is the oldest surviving document of its kind in the entire region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most towns founded before 1841 have surviving records of their founding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Millbrook's municipal records from 1841 onward are completely accurate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Written records are the only reliable evidence of a town's founding date.
