choices.label: E
choices.text: If Millbrook had been founded before 1841, some written record of that founding would have survived to the present.

questions.explanation: The historians infer 'founded in 1841' from 'no surviving document says earlier,' which is an appeal to absent evidence. That inference holds only if an earlier founding would have left a surviving trace. Negate E - suppose Millbrook could have been founded earlier without any record surviving - and the absence of an earlier-dated document proves nothing, so E is required. A compares Millbrook's document to other regional documents, which is irrelevant to Millbrook's own founding date. B speaks only to a general statistical tendency across other towns and doesn't establish what would have happened in Millbrook's specific case, so it's the wrong scope to do the needed work. C concerns the accuracy of later records, not whether any record of an earlier founding would exist, so it's out of scope. D overshoots: the argument doesn't need written records to be the only reliable evidence in general, only that an earlier founding of Millbrook specifically would have produced a surviving one.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Common-law courts have always preferred bright-line rules to flexible standards.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Modern federal procedure has eliminated all procedural barriers facing pro se litigants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drafters of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure rejected the influence of the common-law tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Twombly and Iqbal returned the federal courts to nineteenth-century pleading standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The shift from rigid pleading to notice pleading reflected a deliberate trade of doctrinal predictability for procedural access.

questions.explanation: The passage's central thesis is that the move to notice pleading was a *trade-off*: the drafters knowingly sacrificed some predictability to widen the courthouse door. E captures both halves. A overstates ('always'). B is contradicted by the closing paragraph. C is too strong — the passage says drafters were *informed by* the tradition, not that they rejected it. D confuses the post-Iqbal tightening with a full reversion.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Twombly and Iqbal is best described as one of…

choices.label: A
choices.text: uncritical endorsement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: open hostility.

choices.label: C
choices.text: qualified concern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference.

choices.label: E
choices.text: scholarly bewilderment.

questions.explanation: The author concedes that the cases addressed real problems (mass-tort fishing expeditions) but worries they 'risk reintroducing the very access barrier the 1938 drafters set out to dismantle.' That hedged worry is qualified concern (C), not endorsement, hostility, indifference, or bewilderment.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure took effect in…
questions.explanation: Detail question. The passage states that 'the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure … took effect in 1938.' 1957 is the year of Conley v. Gibson; the other dates appear nowhere as the adoption year.

questions.stem: The author mentions the Field Code of 1848 primarily in order to…

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that fact pleading was superior to the notice pleading that followed it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate an early reform effort that solved some problems but introduced new ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: show that New York courts led all other jurisdictions in procedural innovation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that the writ system was never genuinely abandoned.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that procedural reform inevitably fails.

questions.explanation: The Field Code is introduced as a 'partial remedy' to the writ system, but the next paragraph explains that 'fact pleading … generated its own pathologies.' B captures that role — an early reform that helped yet created new problems. A and E overstate the point; C and D assert claims the passage never makes.

questions.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that defenders of Twombly and Iqbal believe that…

choices.label: A
choices.text: notice pleading should be abolished entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: pro se litigants rarely file meritorious claims.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conley v. Gibson was wrongly decided from the outset.

choices.label: D
choices.text: changes in litigation since 1938 justify a more demanding pleading standard.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the Field Code offered a better model than the Federal Rules.

questions.explanation: Defenders 'note that mass-tort and antitrust complaints had created discovery abuses the 1938 drafters could not have foreseen' — i.e., new litigation conditions warrant a tougher standard, which is D. A, B, C, and E go well beyond anything the defenders are said to claim.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Privity of contract was an indefensible doctrine that nineteenth-century courts should have abandoned far sooner than they did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: American products-liability law moved from a privity bar through negligence to strict liability, yet strict liability retains substantial elements of negligence reasoning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick eliminated the requirement that an injured consumer prove a manufacturer's negligence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Restatement (Second) of Torts settled the long-running dispute over the proper basis of manufacturer liability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola was the most influential single opinion in the history of American tort law.

questions.explanation: The passage traces an arc — privity bar, then negligence after MacPherson, then strict liability — and closes by stressing that strict liability still 'sits uneasily' with negligence reasoning. B captures both the arc and that tension. A states an evaluative claim the author never makes. C is false: the passage says MacPherson 'did not abolish the need to prove fault.' D is contradicted by the final paragraph, which says the question is still 'debatable.' E overstates a detail and is not the passage's overall point.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the doctrine of privity of contract was crystallized in which one of the following cases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Winterbottom v. Wright.

choices.label: B
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Escola v. Coca-Cola Bottling Co.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greenman v. Yuba Power Products.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conley v. Gibson.

questions.explanation: Detail question. The first paragraph states that privity of contract was 'crystallized in the English case Winterbottom v. Wright (1842).' MacPherson (B) cracked the privity rule; Escola (C) and Greenman (D) belong to the strict-liability story; Conley v. Gibson (E) is a civil-procedure case that does not appear in this passage at all.

questions.stem: The author refers to Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that strict liability had already become the governing rule by 1944.

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify an early judicial argument for strict liability that courts would adopt only later.

choices.label: C
choices.text: criticize the Escola majority for reasoning that was internally inconsistent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that Cardozo's approach in MacPherson had been formally overruled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that risk distribution is an inadequate justification for liability.

questions.explanation: The passage presents the 1944 concurrence as urging a change that 'prevailed a generation later' in Greenman (1963) and §402A (1965) — i.e., an early argument adopted only afterward, which is B. A misreads the timeline (it was a concurrence, not the governing rule). C and D describe moves the author never makes. E states a critique the author raises only as one side of a 'debatable' question, not the reason for citing Traynor.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward describing modern products-liability law as 'strict' is best characterized as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic agreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured skepticism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: outright rejection of strict liability as a concept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference to how the doctrine is labeled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: nostalgia for the privity requirement.

questions.explanation: In the final paragraph the author concedes strict liability's risk-distribution rationale but warns that the 'strict-liability label can obscure how much negligence reasoning survives within it' — a hedged, doubting stance toward the label, i.e., measured skepticism (B). A is too positive. C overstates: the author questions the label, not the doctrine's existence. D is wrong because the author plainly cares about the label's accuracy. E finds no support; the author calls privity a remedyless 'price' borne by consumers.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the appellate court in People v. Collins reversed the conviction on which one of the following grounds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The underlying trait frequencies were unproven, and they were multiplied together as if each trait were independent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The one-in-twelve-million figure was too small to support any inference of guilt.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Statistical evidence is categorically inadmissible in criminal trials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The eyewitnesses' descriptions of the couple conflicted with one another.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The prosecution introduced no physical evidence linking the couple to the crime.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that the court reversed because the individual frequencies 'were never established by evidence' and that multiplying them 'assumed, without proof, that each trait was statistically independent.' A restates exactly that ground. B misreads the objection — the court faulted the figure's foundation, not its size, and the passage never says a small probability cannot support an inference. C overstates: the paragraph on DNA shows statistics are not categorically barred. D and E describe facts (conflicting descriptions, missing physical evidence) the passage never mentions.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the doctrine of prior appropriation differs from the riparian doctrine in that prior appropriation

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats flowing water as a resource held in common by every landowner the stream touches.

choices.label: B
choices.text: forbids any user from depleting the flow so as to defeat a neighbor's reasonable use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: assigns water rights to whoever first diverted the water to a beneficial use, independent of land ownership.

choices.label: D
choices.text: allocates water through time-limited permits issued by an administrative agency.

choices.label: E
choices.text: guarantees every claimant a proportional share of the water during a shortage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that prior appropriation 'severed water rights from land ownership entirely and awarded them instead to whoever first diverted the water and put it to a recognized beneficial use.' C restates exactly that. A and B describe the riparian doctrine of paragraph 1 (water 'held in common' and the bar on so depleting the flow as 'to defeat a neighbor's reasonable use'), not appropriation. D describes the regulated-riparian permit regime of paragraph 3, not appropriation. E is contradicted: under appropriation a senior holder 'took a full allotment while junior holders received nothing,' so no proportional share is guaranteed.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Court of King's Bench relied on a legal fiction in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: codify a rule that the legislature had declined to enact

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceal from the public the identity of the judges who governed them

choices.label: C
choices.text: hear cases that would otherwise have fallen outside its authority

choices.label: D
choices.text: relieve overcrowding among the prisoners in its custody

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that a fictitious trespass was itself an actionable wrong

questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains that the King's Bench 'could ordinarily try only prisoners already in its custody, so it invented the supposition' of a fictitious trespass — a pretense that 'quietly extended the court's reach far beyond its original bounds.' (C) captures exactly this jurisdiction-expanding purpose and is correct. (A) fails because the passage says 'no statute authorized the maneuver'; the fiction substituted for legislation rather than codifying any rule the legislature had refused to pass. (B) imports Bentham's later charge of deceit, but the paragraph describes the aim as enlarging authority, not hiding the judges' identities. (D) misreads the 'custody,' which was itself the fiction — the court was not thinning out real prisoners. (E) inverts the device: the trespass was a pretense used to reach the case, not a wrong the court sought to establish as actionable.

questions.stem: The author refers to People v. Collins primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: prove that eyewitness identifications are inherently unreliable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate how the appearance of mathematical precision can lend false certainty to an unsupported factual premise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: establish that appellate courts rarely disturb jury verdicts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: endorse the prosecution's method of multiplying trait frequencies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that criminal convictions require a higher probability than civil liability.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 presents Collins 'as a caution against the aura of certainty that a large number can lend to a shaky factual premise' — precisely the role B names. A misidentifies the lesson as being about eyewitness reliability rather than the misuse of probability. C asserts a claim the passage never makes, and Collins was itself a reversal. D reverses the author's stance; both the court and the author criticize the multiplication. E imports the criminal-versus-civil burden contrast, which belongs to the gatecrasher discussion, not to why Collins is cited.

questions.stem: According to the passage, proponents of actuarial risk-assessment instruments claim that the instruments do which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eliminate the need for a judge to review a defendant's case file.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply a uniform standard to defendants whose circumstances are alike.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Guarantee that no defendant will be wrongly detained before trial.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Predict rearrest more accurately than any human expert could.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Remove race entirely from bail and sentencing decisions.

questions.explanation: The second paragraph credits the instruments with the ability to 'impose a welcome consistency, ensuring that similarly situated defendants are scored by the same yardstick,' which is precisely (B). (A) is never claimed; the case file is mentioned only as part of the older discretionary practice. (C) overstates; nothing in the passage promises a guarantee against wrongful detention. (D) overshoots the modest claim that an instrument can 'flag patterns that an overworked judge... will miss'—that is not a claim of superiority over any human expert. (E) is contradicted by the third paragraph, where the author says the proxies actually track race rather than removing it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Legal fictions are defensible devices whose value depends on their remaining openly recognized as fictions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Legal fictions were indispensable to the early common law but have no place in a modern codified system.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bentham and Fuller reached incompatible conclusions only because they examined different historical periods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fiction of corporate personhood shows why courts should abandon metaphorical reasoning altogether.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Judicial lawmaking is illegitimate whenever it proceeds by way of a fiction rather than open declaration.

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph states the thesis: the author 'leans toward Fuller, but with a qualification' — a fiction 'is worth its cost only so long as it remains visible as a fiction,' since a labeled fiction 'invites the very reform Bentham wanted' while a hardened one 'buries a contestable policy choice.' (A) states exactly this and is correct. (B) echoes Bentham's position, which the author rejects, and the author never says fictions lack a modern place. (C) seizes on the detail that Fuller wrote 'a century later,' but the passage never blames their disagreement on differing eras, and this is not the central claim. (D) misuses the corporate-personhood example, which Fuller offers to show fictions can honestly express, not to condemn metaphor. (E) restates Bentham's rejected view that fiction-based lawmaking is inherently illegitimate.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Bentham would most likely have regarded a legal system's continued reliance on fictions as evidence that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the system's judges were unusually inventive

choices.label: B
choices.text: the system had successfully avoided unjust outcomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: the system relied too heavily on its legislature

choices.label: D
choices.text: the system's litigants preferred flexibility to predictability

choices.label: E
choices.text: the system's written law had not yet been adequately reformed

questions.explanation: Paragraph two reports Bentham's view that a fiction 'was always a confession of failure — proof that the written law had grown inadequate,' and that a codified system 'would dispense with fictions entirely; their persistence was a symptom of arrested legal development.' Combining these, continued reliance on fictions signals to Bentham that the written law remains unreformed, so (E) is correct. (A) contradicts the text, which says persistence was 'not a sign of judicial ingenuity.' (B) overreads: Bentham condemned fictions and would not treat their survival as proof that injustice had been avoided. (C) reverses his commitments — he favored legislative codification and viewed fictions as a sign of too little legislative reform, not excessive reliance on the legislature. (D) attributes the practice to litigants' tastes, a cause the passage never mentions.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Bentham's critique of legal fictions is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: complete agreement with both its conclusion and its reasoning

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismissal of it as wholly without foundation

choices.label: C
choices.text: neutrality born of an unwillingness to take sides

choices.label: D
choices.text: partial validation of its underlying worry combined with rejection of its diagnosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: admiration for its rhetorical force but indifference to its substance

questions.explanation: In the final paragraph the author writes that 'Bentham's alarm, then, is not baseless; it simply misidentifies the culprit,' locating the fault in 'the profession's habit of mistaking a useful metaphor for a discovery' rather than in fictions themselves. That is partial endorsement of the worry plus rejection of the diagnosis, so (D) is correct. (A) is too strong — the author sides with Fuller and rejects Bentham's diagnosis. (B) is refuted directly by 'not baseless.' (C) misreads the author, who plainly 'leans toward Fuller' rather than remaining neutral. (E) is unsupported: the author engages Bentham's substance closely, correcting rather than ignoring it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts should abandon their resistance to statistical evidence, which rests on nothing more than innumeracy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People v. Collins demonstrates that probability calculations have no legitimate role in the courtroom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The law's wariness toward naked statistics is best understood as a demand for individualized, methodologically transparent proof rather than an aversion to numbers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: DNA profiling has resolved the long-standing debate over the admissibility of statistical evidence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The civil preponderance standard should be raised above the 0.501 threshold to prevent unjust verdicts.

questions.explanation: The thesis emerges across paragraphs 3 and 4: the law's resistance 'defends this demand for particularized evidence' and is 'not a superstition about digits,' and quantified proof 'earns its place when its method is auditable and its inference individualized.' C captures both halves. A inverts the author, who endorses the instinct and calls the discomfort 'not mere innumeracy.' B overreads Collins; the DNA example shows numbers can belong in court. D overstates — DNA illustrates the principle rather than resolving the debate. E seizes on the 0.501 detail and urges a reform the passage never proposes.

questions.stem: The discussion of the gatecrasher hypothetical (the rodeo attendees) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide a real case in which a court awarded damages on statistical evidence alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that the preponderance standard is too lenient for civil cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: concede that naked statistical evidence is usually sufficient to prove liability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that a probability can exceed the applicable burden and still fail for want of individualized evidence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: illustrate the transparent methodology that makes DNA evidence acceptable.

questions.explanation: In paragraph 3 the author invokes the 0.501 figure — which 'formally exceeds the civil preponderance standard' — to show that 'what the naked number lacks is individualized proof.' D states that role. A is false twice over: the rodeo case is a hypothetical, not a real case, and no one collects. B misreads the point as a complaint about the standard's leniency rather than about missing particularized evidence. C asserts the reverse of the author's conclusion. E attaches the hypothetical to the DNA methodology discussed later, in paragraph 4.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the current use of actuarial risk-assessment instruments in bail and sentencing is best described as one of…

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved enthusiasm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: bemused detachment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: qualified wariness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: outright condemnation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: complete indifference.

questions.explanation: The author concedes 'the case for these tools is not frivolous' yet insists that 'my reservation is narrower but firm'—a hedged, cautionary stance, i.e., qualified wariness (C). (A) is wrong because the reservation is explicit and firm. (B) fails because the author is engaged and takes a clear side rather than standing amused and aloof. (D) is expressly ruled out by the refusal 'to condemn them wholesale.' (E) is impossible given how much concern the author registers about opacity and biased proxies.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The riparian and prior appropriation doctrines are equally unsuited to every jurisdiction, whatever its climate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Wherever water has grown scarce, prior appropriation should displace the older riparian doctrine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The history of water law shows that no legal rule can allocate a scarce resource fairly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because neither the riparian nor the appropriation doctrine adequately meets modern scarcity, regulated riparianism, despite a genuine cost in predictability, is the better framework.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Administrative permit systems have eliminated the disputes that once arose under the common law of water.

questions.explanation: The passage argues that because neither pure doctrine 'serves a modern jurisdiction well,' regulated riparianism is 'the more promising path,' while conceding that 'predictability has genuine value.' D captures both the rejection of the two older rules and the qualified preference for regulation. A misstates the thesis—the author faults the two doctrines for a modern jurisdiction, not 'equally' and everywhere. B backs the wrong winner: the author prefers regulated riparianism, not prior appropriation. C is contradicted, since the author thinks a scarce resource can be allocated well. E overstates—the passage never claims permit systems have 'eliminated' disputes.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A doctrine is described; a competing doctrine is shown to be superior; the two are then merged into one rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A traditional doctrine is presented; a rival that arose to remedy its limits is introduced; the author advances a synthesizing approach and defends it against an objection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A problem is posed; two failed solutions are catalogued; the author concludes that the problem is insoluble.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A reform is proposed; historical precedents for it are surveyed; the reform is then abandoned in favor of an older rule.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two doctrines are compared; empirical evidence is marshaled to test each; a policy recommendation follows from the data.

questions.explanation: The passage presents the riparian doctrine (paragraph 1), introduces prior appropriation as the rival that 'arose in answer' to riparianism's failure in arid country (paragraph 2), advances regulated riparianism as a synthesis the author endorses (paragraph 3), and defends it against 'the objection most often pressed' (paragraph 4). B tracks that sequence. A is wrong because the rival appropriation doctrine is never shown to be superior. C is wrong because the author treats the problem as soluble, not 'insoluble.' D inverts the structure—no reform is abandoned for an older rule. E is wrong because no empirical evidence or data is marshaled to test the doctrines.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reasonable-person standard should be replaced with a test that measures each defendant against his own capacities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because ordinary morality excuses those who do their best, negligence law is fundamentally unjust to the less capable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although criticized as unfair to those who cannot meet it, the objective standard is best justified as a pragmatic device for allocating the risks of human variation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts have increasingly abandoned the objective standard in favor of individualized inquiries into fault.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The exceptions courts make for children and the suddenly incapacitated show that the objective standard is ultimately incoherent.

questions.explanation: The thesis spans the whole arc: the passage presents the objection (para 2), answers it by recasting the standard as a risk-allocation rule (para 3), and argues the exceptions confirm that logic (para 4). C captures both the criticism and the author's pragmatic defense. A recommends replacing the standard, the opposite of the author's endorsement. B states the critics' position as though it were the author's conclusion. D asserts a wholesale abandonment the passage denies, noting only 'limited' carve-outs. E calls the standard 'incoherent,' but the author says the carve-outs 'confirm the allocative logic.'

questions.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that Fuller would consider the description of a corporation as a 'person' objectionable only if

choices.label: A
choices.text: the legislature had not expressly authorized it

choices.label: B
choices.text: readers came to treat it as a literal fact rather than a shorthand

choices.label: C
choices.text: it were used to enlarge a court's jurisdiction

choices.label: D
choices.text: it appeared in a criminal proceeding rather than a civil one

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bentham's account of judicial deceit turned out to be correct

questions.explanation: Paragraph three says Fuller thought the corporate-'person' fiction 'asserts no falsehood' but warned that a fiction 'can curdle into dogma' when 'later readers may forget the silent "as if" and mistake the metaphor for a fact.' The objection therefore arises only when the shorthand is taken literally, so (B) is correct. (A) states a Benthamite condition — legislative authorization — that Fuller never adopts as his test. (C) borrows the jurisdiction example from paragraph one, which has nothing to do with Fuller's criterion for corporate personhood. (D) invents a civil/criminal distinction the passage never draws. (E) is unsupported: Fuller 'declined to join in the condemnation,' so he does not make his objection depend on Bentham being right.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about a legal fiction whose artificiality has been forgotten?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has achieved the kind of permanence that Bentham thought all sound law should have.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is more likely to prompt legislative reform than a fiction that is openly labeled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It no longer performs the function that led Fuller to defend fictions in the first place.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It exemplifies the honest expression that Fuller distinguished from deception.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It would be endorsed by the author as among the soundest kind of fiction.

questions.explanation: Fuller defended fictions as 'an honest device for saying something new,' one that openly expresses a not-yet-named relationship (paragraph three); the author adds that once a fiction hardens and its artificiality is forgotten, 'it does the opposite' of inviting reform and instead 'buries a contestable policy choice beneath the appearance of settled truth' (paragraph four). Combining the two, a forgotten fiction has stopped doing the transparent, expressive work that justified Fuller's defense, so (C) is correct. (A) misattributes to Bentham a taste for entrenched fictions; he wanted them replaced by open codification, not made permanent. (B) reverses the text — the openly labeled fiction, not the forgotten one, 'invites the very reform Bentham wanted.' (D) describes the honest-expression pole, whereas a forgotten fiction is precisely the case where the 'as if' is lost. (E) contradicts the author, for whom 'the soundest fictions are the ones that announce their own eventual obsolescence,' the opposite of a forgotten one.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the courts' resistance to naked statistical evidence is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified endorsement of every application of the doctrine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: detached neutrality that declines to take any position.

choices.label: C
choices.text: sweeping dismissal of the doctrine as rooted in innumeracy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: alarm that the doctrine has rendered statistical evidence categorically inadmissible.

choices.label: E
choices.text: sustained approval of its core impulse, tempered by concern that it can harden into reflexive hostility.

questions.explanation: The author writes 'I share the courts' underlying instinct' and defends it as principled in paragraph 3, then concedes in paragraph 4 that 'the doctrine can curdle into reflexive hostility, and here the critics have a point.' E captures that approval-with-caveat. A ignores the paragraph 4 concession. B is contradicted by the first-person endorsement. C inverts the author, who says the discomfort 'is not mere innumeracy.' D overstates — the passage notes DNA statistics are 'routinely admit[ted],' so nothing is categorically barred.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about DNA profiling evidence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It would be inadmissible under the reasoning the appellate court applied in Collins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its acceptance shows that the objection to statistical proof was never directed at quantification as such.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It satisfies the individualization concern only because its random-match figure is smaller than the figure in Collins.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has replaced the civil preponderance standard with a probabilistic threshold.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its use has been resisted by courts on the same grounds that doomed the Collins calculation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 observes that DNA evidence 'is every bit as statistical as the one in Collins' yet is admitted because it rests on 'a transparent, replicable methodology' and 'a sample drawn from the defendant himself,' concluding that 'the objection was never to numbers as such.' B is that supported inference. A is contradicted — the passage distinguishes DNA precisely so that Collins-style objections do not reach it. C fixes on magnitude, but the passage grounds the difference in auditable method and individualized source, not the size of the figure. D invents a doctrinal change the passage never mentions. E contradicts the statement that 'courts today routinely admit DNA profiling.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Actuarial risk-assessment instruments should be banned from bail and sentencing decisions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Judicial intuition has proven more reliable than any statistical instrument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Proprietary instruments are unconstitutional because defendants cannot inspect them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Although actuarial instruments could improve on discretionary judgment, their adoption has outrun the safeguards needed to make them trustworthy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The disparities produced by human judges justify replacing them with statistical formulas.

questions.explanation: The passage grants the instruments' promise (paragraph two) but rests on the fourth paragraph's warning that 'the pace of adoption has badly outrun the development of these safeguards'—exactly (D). (A) is contradicted by the author's stated refusal 'to condemn them wholesale.' (B) misreads the passage, which concedes an instrument can catch patterns a judge misses. (C) inflates the opacity concern into a constitutional claim the author never makes. (E) endorses full replacement, whereas the author wants the instruments used only 'as one input among many.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward regulated riparianism is most accurately described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified enthusiasm untroubled by any drawback.

choices.label: B
choices.text: detached neutrality as between it and its rivals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: initial approval that gives way to serious doubt.

choices.label: D
choices.text: skepticism relieved only by grudging acknowledgment of its convenience.

choices.label: E
choices.text: qualified endorsement that acknowledges a genuine cost.

questions.explanation: The author calls regulated riparianism 'the more promising path' and concludes that 'the trade favors regulation,' yet grants that 'predictability has genuine value.' E—qualified endorsement acknowledging a genuine cost—fits precisely. A is wrong because the author expressly concedes a drawback. B is wrong because the author is not neutral but takes a side. C is wrong because the approval never 'gives way' to doubt; the endorsement stands. D reverses the polarity: the author endorses the approach rather than merely tolerating it.

questions.stem: The primary function of the fourth paragraph is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: raise the objection most pressed against the author's preferred approach and then argue that, on balance, it does not defeat that approach.

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce a third doctrine that the earlier paragraphs had not considered.

choices.label: C
choices.text: summarize the historical developments described in the first three paragraphs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: concede that the author's recommendation should ultimately be withdrawn.

choices.label: E
choices.text: supply empirical data confirming the superiority of prior appropriation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens by granting that 'the objection most often pressed against such systems is real'—the loss of predictability—and then answers that 'on balance the trade favors regulation.' A describes exactly that raise-then-rebut move. B is wrong: no new third doctrine is introduced, since regulated riparianism was already presented in paragraph 3. C is wrong because the paragraph argues rather than merely summarizing the history. D is wrong because the author does not withdraw the recommendation but reaffirms it. E is wrong because no empirical data appears, and the paragraph does not favor prior appropriation.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A junior appropriator is guaranteed at least a partial allotment during a shortage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regulated riparian permit systems place an agency's allocation decisions beyond judicial review.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In a region where water is abundant, the riparian doctrine's premise of common sharing is not obviously untenable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prior appropriation emerged in the eastern states before spreading to the arid West.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Under a regulated riparian permit system the reasonableness of a proposed use plays no part in allocation.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 grounds riparianism in the fact that 'water in a well-watered landscape is rarely scarce enough to exhaust,' and paragraph 2 says that 'premise collapses in arid country'; together these support C—where water is abundant the sharing premise remains tenable. A is contradicted: junior holders 'received nothing' in a shortage. B is contradicted: the author notes that 'the agency's decisions are reviewable.' D is contradicted: appropriation 'arose' in 'the mining camps of the nineteenth-century American West,' not first in the East. E is contradicted: 'the reasonableness of the use' is an express permit criterion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, critics of the objective reasonable-person standard object to it primarily on the ground that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: holds defendants liable even when a reasonable person would have acted in exactly the same way.

choices.label: B
choices.text: condemns individuals for limitations they were unable to overcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: requires juries to conduct a searching inquiry into each defendant's personal capacities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: has grown too complicated for modern juries to apply consistently.

choices.label: E
choices.text: excuses careless conduct whenever a defendant can show that he tried his best.

questions.explanation: Paragraph two states the critics' complaint directly: the law holds 'the slow-witted, the inexperienced, and the congenitally clumsy to the same external measure,' 'condemning them for shortcomings they could not have overcome.' B restates exactly that objection. A misdescribes the complaint — critics do not object that identical reasonable conduct yields liability; they object that those who cannot meet the standard are condemned. C inverts the passage: the standard is faulted for refusing to inquire into personal capacities, not for requiring such inquiry. D contradicts paragraph one, which praises the standard as 'administrable.' E describes the moral excuse that the standard pointedly rejects, not the critics' objection to the standard.

questions.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the author would regard actuarial instruments as substantially more acceptable if…

choices.label: A
choices.text: judges were required to defer to the instrument's score in every case.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the instruments were adopted more rapidly and in more jurisdictions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: their scores were kept confidential from defendants to prevent gaming.

choices.label: D
choices.text: proponents stopped comparing them to discretionary judgment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: their methods were opened to independent validation and their bias-laden proxies removed.

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph states the instruments 'might yet deliver' on their promise if 'subjected to independent validation, and stripped of the proxies most likely to smuggle in bias'—directly yielding (E). (A) reverses the author's preference for treating a score as merely 'one input among many.' (B) worsens the very problem the author names: adoption outrunning safeguards. (C) deepens the opacity the author criticizes as shielding instruments 'from the defendants they score.' (D) misses the point; the objection concerns the proxies and secrecy, not the rhetorical comparison.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the proponents' argument that a transparent formula is preferable to unexamined intuition is best characterized as…

choices.label: A
choices.text: acknowledgment of its force coupled with doubt that it settles the matter.

choices.label: B
choices.text: enthusiastic and unqualified agreement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismissal of it as plainly mistaken.

choices.label: D
choices.text: suspicion that it is offered in bad faith.

choices.label: E
choices.text: indifference to whether it is sound.

questions.explanation: The author says proponents 'point out, fairly,' and that 'the formula would seem the safer bet,' granting the argument real force; but the very next paragraph, opening 'Yet the formula is rarely transparent,' shows the author doubts it settles the question—hence (A). (B) ignores that pivot into reservation. (C) contradicts the concession that the point is fair and 'not frivolous.' (D) has no basis; the author never impugns the proponents' motives. (E) is refuted by the sustained, serious engagement the author gives the argument.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the objective reasonable-person standard is best described as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified enthusiasm for the moral rigor it demands of defendants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: deep ambivalence about whether it can be justified at all.

choices.label: C
choices.text: sharp disapproval of the way it treats the less capable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: detached neutrality among competing academic positions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: reasoned endorsement of it as a practical device for allocating risk.

questions.explanation: The author calls the standard a 'sensible' and 'considered decision' and a 'pragmatic instrument,' endorsing it while denying it is a moral verdict. E captures that reasoned, practical endorsement. A is wrong because the author expressly denies the standard rests on moral rigor, insisting it is not 'a pronouncement that she is a bad person.' B overstates his doubt; he is confident, not ambivalent. C attributes to the author the critics' disapproval, which he rejects. D is wrong because the author plainly takes a side rather than standing neutral among positions.

questions.stem: The author's primary purpose in the second paragraph is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: set out the objection that the remainder of the passage is devoted to answering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: concede a genuine flaw in the position the author goes on to defend.

choices.label: C
choices.text: restate the main point that had already been established in the first paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: supply historical evidence for the objective standard's long endurance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: propose a reform that would make the standard sensitive to individual capacity.

questions.explanation: Paragraph two lays out the fairness objection — that the standard 'punishes people not for choosing badly but for being who they are' — which paragraphs three and four then rebut. A captures that setup-for-rebuttal role. B is wrong: the paragraph voices the critics, not a concession by the author, whose genuine concession about 'soft edges' appears in paragraph four. C is wrong because paragraph one does not state the main point, and paragraph two introduces the new critique rather than restating anything. D misassigns the point about the standard's 'century' of use, which belongs to paragraph one. E is wrong because the author never proposes an individualizing reform; he defends the existing standard.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage as a whole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rule is stated, a series of counterexamples is catalogued, and the rule is ultimately abandoned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing standards are compared, and one is shown to be superior on empirical grounds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrine's history is traced from its origins through to its eventual replacement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A standard is described, an objection to it is presented and answered, and apparent exceptions are shown to reinforce that answer.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A moral principle is defended against the charge that it is merely pragmatic.

questions.explanation: The passage describes the objective standard (para 1), presents the fairness objection (para 2), answers it with the allocative account (para 3), and argues the individualized exceptions 'confirm the allocative logic' (para 4). D matches that structure. A is wrong: the rule is defended, not 'abandoned.' B invents a comparison of two competing standards resolved on 'empirical' grounds, which never occurs. C describes a history ending in 'replacement,' but the standard is neither chiefly historical nor replaced. E reverses the author's point — he defends the standard as pragmatic against the assumption that it must be moral, not a moral principle against a charge of pragmatism.

questions.stem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the associates argue, from first to fifth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: F, G, H, J, K

choices.label: B
choices.text: G, F, H, K, J

choices.label: C
choices.text: K, F, H, J, G

choices.label: D
choices.text: F, H, K, J, G

choices.label: E
choices.text: H, F, G, J, K

questions.explanation: Apply the rules as eliminators. A puts F first and H third — not the required immediate F-H block (Rule 1). B places J fifth, violating Rule 2 (J fourth). C starts with K, violating Rule 3. E reverses the block, putting H before F (Rule 1). D — F, H, K, J, G — satisfies all three: F is immediately before H, J is fourth, and K is not first.

questions.stem: If H argues third, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: F argues first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: K argues second.

choices.label: C
choices.text: J argues fifth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: K argues third.

choices.label: E
choices.text: G argues first.

questions.explanation: If H=3, Rule 1 forces F=2. Rule 2 fixes J=4. Slots 1 and 5 remain for G and K, and Rule 3 forbids K=1, so G=1 and K=5. Therefore E — G argues first — must be true. A is false (F=2); B and D misplace K (K=5); C is false (J=4).

questions.stem: If G argues fifth, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: K argues third.

choices.label: B
choices.text: H argues first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: J argues fifth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: F argues second.

choices.label: E
choices.text: K argues first.

questions.explanation: If G=5, the F-H block (Rule 1) and J=4 (Rule 2) leave only one valid layout: F=1, H=2, K=3, J=4, G=5. So A — K argues third — must be true. E is forbidden by Rule 3; B, C, and D are inconsistent with the forced layout.

A is false because F is first, B is false because G is second, D is false because J is fourth (K, not J, is fifth), and E is false because M is sixth.

Because Rule 2 puts N before R, R can never lead; R occupies slot 3, 5, or 6 in every order, so A must be true. B fails in the first and third orders, where L is sixth. So A must be true. B (G) holds only in {G, J, L} and fails in {J, K, L}. C (K) holds only in {J, K, L} and fails in {G, J, L}. D (F) is impossible, since F would require H while Rule 3 keeps H out. Placing F-G in 5-6 would make F fifth, but then H (which follows F by Rule 4) and the whole H-J block would have no room, so F-G must take slots 1-2. Therefore F is first and G is second, and E, 'F argues first,' must be true — the only orders are F-G-K-H-J-M and F-G-K-M-H-J. A ('H fourth'), B ('M sixth'), and D ('J fifth') hold only in the first order; C ('H fifth') holds only in the second; none of those four must be true.

A (F) is false in {G, H, L}. B (G) is false in {F, H, L}. C (L) is false in {F, G, H}. E (H) is false in {G, J, L}, where J supplies the disjunct instead.

In the first the M-P block fills slots 2 and 3, pushing N and R to 5 and 6; in the second the block fills 5 and 6, pushing N and R to 2 and 3. Either way N sits immediately before R, so E must be true. A, B, and C each hold only in (L,M,P,T,N,R); in the other order M is fifth, P is sixth, and R is third. By Rule 4, F argues before H, and since H cannot take G's slot, H must be at least two slots after F — hence later than G. So B, 'G argues before H,' holds in every valid order and must be true. The others each fail in some valid order: A ('K before F') is false in F-G-H-J-K-M; C ('H before K') is false in F-G-K-H-J-M; D ('F before K') is false in K-F-G-H-J-M; and E ('M after J') is false in F-G-K-M-H-J, where M is fourth and J is sixth.

In the first three M precedes R; in the fourth M (fifth) follows R (third), but there L (first) precedes R, so in every order M or L precedes R, and C must be true. A fails in the fourth order (M after R). B fails there too (P sixth, after R). D fails in the second order, where N is fifth, after T. E fails in the fourth order, where R (third) precedes T (fourth).

guides.method: Rule-by-rule elimination on an ordering game

steps.title: Name the game
steps.text: Five entities, five slots, one each — a pure ordering (sequencing) game. For a 'could be the order' question, you never need a full solve: each rule eliminates the answer choices that break it.

steps.title: Write out the elements
steps.text: List the roster and the board before touching the rules: associates F, G, H, J, K into slots 1–5. Writing the inventory first is what lets you see leftovers later.

representation.note: Empty board — inventory only. Slots run left to right, first to last.

steps.title: Symbolize each rule
steps.text: Turn every rule into notation you can scan in one glance. An 'immediately before' rule is a block; a fixed slot is an equation; a forbidden slot is a strike-out.

rules.note: A block: F and H are adjacent, F on the left. They move together.
Fixed placement — write J straight onto the board.
An exclusion — mark slot 1 with ~K.

steps.title: Sketch the board
steps.text: Put the fixed and forbidden marks on the board. J owns slot 4; slot 1 bars K. The [F H] block floats — it needs two adjacent open slots, so it must fit in 1–2, 2–3, or… not 4–5 (J blocks 4).

representation.note: The [F H] block can only occupy slots 1–2 or 2–3.

steps.title: Run each rule against the choices
steps.text: Take one rule at a time and cross off violators. Rule 1 [F H]: choice A splits F and H (F first, H third) and choice E reverses them — gone. Rule 2 J = 4: choice B puts J fifth — gone. Rule 3 K ≠ 1: choice C opens with K — gone. An elimination grid makes the sweep mechanical.

cells.note: F and H are not adjacent.

representation.note: Rows are answer choices; columns are rules. One 'no' kills a row.

steps.title: One choice survives
steps.text: Only D remains: F, H, K, J, G. Check it once — F immediately before H (slots 1–2), J fourth, K second (not first). Every rule holds, so D is correct.

guides.method: Chain forced placements from a local condition

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If H argues third…' is a local question: it adds a temporary condition. Redraw the board with the new fact and chase every consequence before reading a single answer choice.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Same game, same notation. Keep the three rules in view — the new condition will interact with all of them.

steps.title: Place the condition
steps.text: Drop H into slot 3. The block [F H] instantly forces F into slot 2 — that is the whole point of symbolizing adjacency as a block. J was already fixed in slot 4.

representation.note: H = 3 (given) drags F to 2 via the [F H] block.

steps.title: Chase the leftovers
steps.text: Only G and K remain, and only slots 1 and 5 are open. K ≠ 1 forbids K from slot 1, so K takes 5 and G takes 1. The entire order is forced: G, F, H, J, K.

representation.note: Fully determined — a must-be-true question with one possible world.

steps.title: Match the forced board to the choices
steps.text: G argues first, so E must be true. The wrong answers contradict the forced board: F is second (not first, killing A), K is fifth (killing B and D), and J is fourth (killing C).

guides.method: Chain forced placements from a local condition

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If G argues fifth…' is a local question. Redraw the board with G in slot 5 and chase every consequence before touching the choices.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Same game, same notation — keep all three rules in view.

rules.note: Adjacent block, F left.
Fixed — write it on the board.
Mark slot 1 with ~K.

steps.title: Place the condition
steps.text: Put G in slot 5. J was already fixed in slot 4. That leaves slots 1, 2, and 3 for F, H, and K — and the [F H] block needs two of them, adjacent.

representation.note: Only slots 1–3 remain open, and [F H] must fit inside them.

steps.title: Chase the leftovers
steps.text: The [F H] block can sit in 1–2 or 2–3. If it took 2–3, K would be forced into slot 1 — forbidden by K ≠ 1. So the block takes 1–2, and K takes the only seat left, slot 3. The whole order is forced: F, H, K, J, G.

representation.note: One possible world — a must-be-true question with a fully forced board.

steps.title: Match the forced board
steps.text: K argues third, so A must be true. The wrong answers contradict the forced order: H is second, F is first, J is fourth, and K ≠ 1 already barred K from opening.

guides.method: Enumerate the valid worlds, then test the extremes

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'CANNOT be true' is a global question: the right answer fails in every valid order, and each wrong answer succeeds in at least one. When a game is small, listing the valid orders outright is the fastest weapon.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Three rules, five slots — this game is tightly constrained, so a full enumeration will be short.

rules.note: Adjacent block, F left.
Fixed — write it on the board.
Mark slot 1 with ~K.

steps.title: Where can the [F H] block go?
steps.text: J owns slot 4, so the block cannot use 3–4 or 4–5. That leaves [F H] in slots 1–2 or 2–3. Everything else follows from that split.

representation.note: Block windows: 1–2 or 2–3. Note what that does to H — it can only ever sit in slot 2 or slot 3.

steps.title: List every valid order
steps.text: Block in 1–2: G and K fill 3 and 5 in either order — two worlds. Block in 2–3: K ≠ 1 forces G into slot 1 and K into slot 5 — one world. Three valid orders total.

steps.title: Test the choices against the three worlds
steps.text: H sits in slot 2 or 3 in every world, so 'H argues first' can never happen — B cannot be true. Each other choice occurs somewhere: K fifth (world 1), G third (world 2), F second (world 3), K third (world 1).

guides.method: Chain forced placements from a local condition

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If K argues third…' is a local question: add the condition to the board and push the rules until nothing else moves.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Keep the three rules in front of you — the block is the engine here.

rules.note: Adjacent block, F left.
Fixed — write it on the board.
Mark slot 1 with ~K.

steps.title: Place the condition
steps.text: K takes slot 3 and J was already fixed in slot 4. Now ask: where can the [F H] block still fit? It needs two adjacent open slots.

representation.note: Open slots: 1, 2, 5. The only adjacent pair is 1–2.

steps.title: The block has one home
steps.text: Slots 1–2 are the only adjacent open pair, so F takes 1 and H takes 2. G inherits the last seat, slot 5. The order is fully forced: F, H, K, J, G.

representation.note: Fully determined — exactly one world satisfies the condition.

steps.title: Match the forced board
steps.text: G argues fifth, so C must be true. Against the forced order the others fail: H is second (not first, not fourth), F is first (not second), and G is fifth (not first).

guides.method: Block-and-order elimination on a six-slot sequence

steps.title: Write out the elements
steps.text: Six students — F, G, H, J, K, M — into slots 1 through 6, one each. Bigger board, same discipline: inventory first.

representation.note: Empty six-slot board.

steps.title: Symbolize: two blocks, two orderings
steps.text: Two adjacency blocks and two loose before/after rules. Note the difference in notation — a dash (K … M) allows any gap; a block [F G] allows none. Rule 4 chains the blocks: the [F G] block sits somewhere before the [H J] block.

rules.note: Adjacent, F left.
Adjacent, H left.

rules.rule_text: K argues at some time before M.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.

rules.rule_text: F argues at some time before H.
rules.note: Combining with the blocks: the F-G pair precedes the H-J pair.

steps.title: One rule at a time across the choices
steps.text: Rule 4 (F before H): choice A opens with H, J — dead. Rule 1 [F G]: choice C wedges K between F and G — dead. Rule 2 [H J]: choice D separates H (slot 3) from J (slot 5) — dead. Rule 3 K — M: choice E puts K sixth, after M — dead.

steps.title: Verify the survivor
steps.text: B — F, G, K, H, J, M — passes every rule: [F G] in 1–2, [H J] in 4–5, K (3) before M (6), F (1) before H (4). B is correct.

guides.method: Rule-by-rule elimination on an ordering game

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: An 'acceptable order' question: no solving needed. Take one rule at a time and cross off every choice that breaks it — exactly one will survive.

steps.title: Write out the elements
steps.text: Six witnesses — L, M, N, P, R, T — into sessions 1 through 6. T is already pinned to session 4 and L is restricted to the edges.

representation.note: L may only take session 1 or 6.

steps.title: Symbolize each rule
steps.text: Four rules: a block, a loose ordering, a fixed seat, and an either/or edge rule.

rules.note: Adjacent block, M left.

rules.rule_text: N testifies at some time before R.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.
Fixed — the board's anchor.
L brackets the schedule — split into two worlds.

steps.title: Sweep the choices one rule at a time
steps.text: Apply [M P] first, then N — R, then T = 4, then the L edge rule. Each rule knocks out at least one listed order; keep a tally rather than re-checking whole orders.

steps.title: The survivor
steps.text: N, M, P, T, R, L passes every rule — M immediately before P (sessions 2–3), N (1) before R (5), T fourth, L sixth — so C is correct. The others each break exactly one rule: a split M/P pair, R before N, T in the wrong session, or L stuck in the middle.

guides.method: Find the hidden parity constraint

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'Each could be true EXCEPT' means four choices happen in some valid order and one never does. Look for a structural constraint — often a slot an entity can never occupy.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Two adjacency blocks plus two ordering rules. Blocks eat pairs of consecutive slots — that geometry is the key.

rules.note: Adjacent, F left.
Adjacent, H left.

rules.rule_text: K argues at some time before M.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.

rules.rule_text: F argues at some time before H.
rules.note: The F-G block sits somewhere before the H-J block.

steps.title: Watch what the blocks do to M
steps.text: The two blocks [F G] and [H J] occupy two disjoint pairs of consecutive slots, and K precedes M. Try to build any valid order and track where M lands: the blocks tile the row so tightly that K and M are forced into the leftover pair of slots, with M after K.

representation.note: Six slots, two 2-slot blocks, and the K–M pair: three 'units' of width 2 filling the row.

steps.title: M's possible seats
steps.text: Treat [F G], [H J], and (K…M) as three width-2 units. However you arrange them, M sits at the right edge of its unit — an even slot. Enumerate: M can testify second, fourth, or sixth, never in an odd slot.

rules.symbols: K M | F G | H J  →  M = 2
F G | K M | H J  →  M = 4
F G | H J | K M  →  M = 6

steps.title: Apply the parity fact
steps.text: M can never argue third — an odd slot — so D is the exception. The rest all occur: F first and G second in most worlds, H fourth in F-G-K-H-J-M, K fifth in F-G-H-J-K-M.

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If K argues fifth…' is a local question. Place K, then let the ordering rules squeeze everything else.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Two blocks and two ordering rules — note the derived rule: the F-G block precedes the H-J block.

Adjacent, H left.

steps.title: Place the condition and push K — M
steps.text: K in slot 5 leaves only slot 6 after it, so M must be sixth. Slots 1–4 are now exactly four seats for the two blocks.

representation.note: Blocks [F G] and [H J] must tile slots 1–4.

steps.title: Order the blocks
steps.text: F argues before H, so the F-G block takes 1–2 and the H-J block takes 3–4. The full order is forced: F, G, H, J, K, M.

representation.note: One world — every seat is decided.

steps.title: Match the forced board
steps.text: H argues third, so C must be true. Against the forced order: F is first, G is second, J is fourth, and M is sixth — each wrong choice contradicts a forced seat.

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: An 'acceptable list' question on an in/out selection game. No deductions needed — run each conditional rule against the five listed rosters and cross off violators.

steps.title: Symbolize each conditional with its contrapositive

steps.title: Sweep the choices one rule at a time
steps.text: Rule 1 (F → H): cross off any roster showing F without H. Rule 2 (G → ¬K): cross off any roster with both G and K. Rule 3 (H → ¬J): cross off any roster with both H and J. Count what falls to each.

steps.title: The survivor
steps.text: G, H, and L is the only roster that violates nothing: no F (Rule 1 idle), G in with K out, H in with J out — so B is correct. Two choices pair F without H, one pairs G with K, and one pairs H with J.

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'CANNOT both be displayed' asks for a forbidden pair. A rule of the form X → ¬Y bans the pair {X, Y} outright — check the rules before testing anything by hand.

steps.title: Symbolize each conditional with its contrapositive
steps.text: Two of the three rules are direct incompatibilities; the F rule is a requirement, not a ban.

steps.title: Which pairs do the rules actually forbid?
steps.text: G → ¬K bans {G, K}. H → ¬J bans {H, J}. Nothing else is banned by a single rule — F → H permits F and H together (in fact it demands H when F is in). Any pair not on the banned list can usually be realized in some legal roster.

cells.note: Free agent — no rule touches L.

representation.note: Forbidden pairs from the arrows: {G,K} and {H,J}.

steps.title: Match the banned pair to the choices
steps.text: G and K can never both hang — Rule 2 says so directly — making D the credited pair. Each other pair co-exists in a legal roster: F with H in {F,G,H}, H with L in {F,H,L}, J with L in {G,J,L}, K with L in {H,K,L}.

steps.title: Read the question type

steps.title: Look at session 1 across all four
steps.text: The first session is always M, N, or L. R never leads — it always needs N somewhere before it, and the surviving layouts put R in session 3, 5, or 6.

steps.title: Match against the choices
steps.text: R never testifies first, so A must be true. Every other claim fails in at least one order: L sixth (not first) in two worlds, N floats between sessions 1, 2, 3 and 5, P can land second or third, and M leads only one world.

guides.method: Fire the contrapositives, then count the seats

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If J is displayed…' is a local question on a selection game. Fire every contrapositive the condition triggers, then check who is left to fill the remaining seats.

steps.title: Symbolize each conditional with its contrapositive
steps.text: You will use the flipped forms here, not the originals.

rules.rule_text: If F is displayed, then H is displayed.

rules.note: H and J can never both be in.

steps.title: Chain from J in
steps.text: J in fires J → ¬H: H is out. H out fires ¬H → ¬F: F is out. Two of the three display seats remain, and only G, K, and L are still eligible.

representation.note: Two open seats, three candidates — and one pair of them is banned.

steps.title: Count the ways to fill two seats
steps.text: The two remaining seats come from {G, K, L}, but G and K cannot sit together (Rule 2). The only legal pairs are {G, L} and {K, L}. Notice what both have in common.

steps.title: The common member
steps.text: Both legal completions include L, so 'L is displayed' — choice A — must be true. G and K each appear in only one completion, and F and H were knocked out by the contrapositive chain before the seats were even counted.

guides.method: Test the block's remaining windows

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If K argues third…' is a local question. K in slot 3 splits the row and shrinks the windows where each block can fit — test them.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: The derived rule matters again: [F G] must finish before [H J] begins.

Adjacent, H left.

steps.title: Place the condition
steps.text: K takes slot 3. The [F G] block now needs two adjacent open slots: the candidates are 1–2, 4–5, and 5–6.

representation.note: Where can [F G] still fit? Test each window against F — H.

steps.title: Kill the late windows
steps.text: If [F G] sat in 4–5 or 5–6, then H — which must come after F with the whole [H J] block behind it — would have at most one slot left. Impossible. So [F G] takes 1–2: F first, G second. The two survivors are F-G-K-H-J-M and F-G-K-M-H-J.

representation.note: Slots 4–6 hold [H J] and M, in either arrangement that keeps K before M.

steps.title: Find what holds in both worlds
steps.text: F argues first in both surviving orders, so E must be true. The other placements each hold in only one of the two worlds — H fourth, M sixth, and J fifth only in the first; H fifth only in the second.

guides.method: Follow the forced chain from the supposition

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'Assuming F is displayed, each could also be displayed EXCEPT' — fire F's consequences first; the exception will be whoever those consequences lock out.

steps.title: Symbolize each conditional with its contrapositive
steps.text: F is the trigger of Rule 1 — start the chain there.

steps.title: Chain from F in
steps.text: F in fires F → H: H is displayed. H in fires H → ¬J: J is out. One display seat remains for G, K, or L (G and K still cannot pair, but only one seat is open anyway).

representation.note: The chain F ⇒ H ⇒ ¬J runs before any choice is read.

steps.title: The locked-out painting
steps.text: J can never join F — the chain F → H → ¬J bars it — so C is the exception. Each remaining painting fills the third seat in some legal roster: G in {F,G,H}, K in {F,H,K}, L in {F,H,L}, and H is displayed in all of them.

guides.method: Prove a disjunction by contradiction

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If K is not displayed…' is a local question, and one choice is a disjunction ('at least one of…'). The standard proof: suppose the disjunction fails and show the rules collapse.

steps.title: Symbolize each conditional with its contrapositive
steps.text: Keep the contrapositive of Rule 1 in view — it delivers the contradiction.

rules.rule_text: If F is displayed, then H is displayed.
rules.note: Write every conditional with its contrapositive.

rules.rule_text: If G is displayed, then K is not displayed.
rules.note: G and K can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: If H is displayed, then J is not displayed.
rules.note: H and J can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: Exactly three of the six are displayed.
rules.note: A selection (in/out) game, not an ordering game.

steps.title: Suppose H and J are BOTH out
steps.text: With K also out, three of the six paintings are gone, so the display would have to be exactly the remaining three: F, G, and L. But F displayed fires F → H, and H is out — contradiction. The supposition dies.

cells.note: Forced in… but F → H fails!

representation.note: Three exclusions force the other three in — and the forced roster breaks Rule 1.

steps.title: State what the contradiction proves
steps.text: H and J cannot both sit out when K is out, so at least one of them is displayed — D must be true. The single-painting claims all fail in some legal world: no F in {G,H,L}, no G in {F,H,L}, no L in {F,G,H}, and no H in {G,J,L}, where J carries the disjunct.

guides.method: Split into the two surviving worlds

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If L testifies first…' is a local question that halves the game. Build both surviving worlds fully — the answer must hold in each.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: With L pinned to session 1, only the [M P] block placement still varies.

steps.title: Place the condition
steps.text: L first, T fourth. The open seats are 2, 3, 5, 6, and the [M P] block needs an adjacent pair: 2–3 or 5–6.

representation.note: Two block windows → two worlds to build.

steps.title: Build both worlds
steps.text: Block in 2–3: N and R take 5 and 6 with N first → L, M, P, T, N, R. Block in 5–6: N and R take 2 and 3 with N first → L, N, R, T, M, P. Compare the two: in both, N sits in the session immediately before R.

steps.title: Find the invariant
steps.text: N testifies immediately before R in both worlds, so E must be true. The other claims each hold in only one world — M second, P third, R sixth in the first; and M before N fails outright in the second, where N is second and M fifth.

guides.method: Derive a relational fact from the blocks

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: A global 'must be true' with relational choices (X before Y). Don't enumerate every order — derive the relationship directly from the rules.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Focus on how [F G] interacts with F — H.

Adjacent, H left.

steps.title: Chain the two rules
steps.text: G sits in the slot immediately after F. H comes after F too — but H cannot take G's slot (G is there). So H is at least two slots after F, which puts H after G in every valid order.

rules.rule_text: G's seat is pinned to F's.

rules.note: G always testifies before H — a derived rule the choices will probe.

steps.title: Apply the derived rule
steps.text: G argues before H in every valid order, so B must be true. Each other relational claim fails somewhere: K can follow F (F-G-H-J-K-M), H can follow K (F-G-K-H-J-M), K can lead (K-F-G-H-J-M puts K before F), and M can precede J (F-G-K-M-H-J).

guides.method: Test a disjunctive claim across every world

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: A global 'must be true' whose choices include an either/or. Disjunctions are weaker claims — easier to make true everywhere — so expect the credited answer to be one. Enumerate the worlds first.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Same anchors: T = 4, L on an edge, [M P] block, N — R.

steps.title: The four valid orders
steps.text: Two L-worlds times two block windows gives four orders. Write them down once.

N M P T R L
L M P T N R
