steps.title: Track R's predecessors
steps.text: In the first three orders M testifies before R. The fourth order (L, N, R, T, M, P) breaks that — M comes after R — but there L leads, so L precedes R instead. In every world, at least one of M and L is before R.

steps.title: Match the disjunction
steps.text: 'M before R, or L before R' survives all four orders, so C must be true. The stronger single claims each die in the fourth order — M and P both follow R there — while the remaining choices fail elsewhere: N can follow T, and T can follow R.

guides.method: Abstract the argument's form, then match it

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'Most similar in its reasoning' is a parallel-reasoning question. The content (law firms, supreme courts) is a distraction — only the argument's skeleton matters. Extract the form before reading any choice.

steps.title: Map the argument
steps.text: Two premises feed one conclusion: a universal rule about a group, plus a membership claim placing Maria in the group.

nodes.text: Every senior partner has argued before the state supreme court.
Maria has argued before the state supreme court.

steps.title: Reduce to symbols
steps.text: Strip the content away entirely. This is universal instantiation — a valid form. Your job is now to find the choice with exactly this notation, and to reject choices whose notation differs.

rules.rule_text: Every senior partner has argued at the supreme court.
rules.note: P = senior partner, Q = has argued there.
Valid: universal instantiation.

steps.title: Match forms, not topics
steps.text: B swaps 'all' for 'most' — probabilistic, not universal. C runs the conditional backward (affirming the consequent: Q, therefore P). D does the same trick with an if-then. E reasons from a negative universal to a 'might' — no instantiation at all. Each fails on form, not subject matter.

steps.title: The matching skeleton
steps.text: A — all birds have feathers; a penguin is a bird; so a penguin has feathers — is 'All P are Q; x is P; ∴ x is Q' exactly. A is correct.

guides.method: Find the causal leap, then supply the alternative cause

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A weaken question. First isolate the conclusion and the evidence; the gap between them is where the correct answer will strike.

steps.title: Map the argument
steps.text: The planner's evidence is a correlation across other cities; the conclusion is a causal prediction about this one. Notice the unstated assumption doing the real work.

nodes.text: Every comparable city that built light rail saw congestion fall within five years.
(Unstated) The rail line itself caused those congestion drops.
Building light rail here will reduce downtown congestion.

steps.title: Attack the assumption
steps.text: Correlation-to-causation arguments break when something else could explain the observed effect. To weaken, look for an answer that supplies a rival cause for the congestion drop in those comparable cities — not one that quibbles about cost, popularity, or engineering.

steps.title: Discard the off-point choices
steps.text: A (cost) changes the price, not the congestion logic. B (construction noise) is irrelevant to whether rail reduces traffic. C (rider satisfaction) mildly supports the planner. E (underground routing) says nothing about the causal claim. None touches the assumption.

steps.title: The rival cause
steps.text: D reveals that every comparable city also enacted congestion-pricing tolls — a confound that could explain the entire congestion drop without the rail line. That severs evidence from conclusion, so D most weakens the argument.

guides.method: Symbolize the conditional, apply the contrapositive

steps.title: Spot the conditional
steps.text: One if-then plus one fact. Any 'properly concluded' question over a conditional is asking whether you can run modus ponens or modus tollens — and only those. Symbolize before judging any choice.

steps.title: Write the rule and its contrapositive
steps.text: Translate the sentence into arrow notation, then write the contrapositive immediately — on the LSAT the contrapositive is usually the version you will actually use.

rules.rule_text: If the contract is enforceable, then it was signed by both parties.
rules.note: E = enforceable, S = signed by both.
Flip and negate both sides.

rules.rule_text: The contract was not signed by both parties.
rules.note: The given fact — it matches the contrapositive's trigger.

steps.title: Fire the contrapositive
steps.text: ¬S is exactly the left side of ¬S → ¬E, so ¬E follows: the contract is not enforceable. This is modus tollens. Note what you may NOT do: from E → S alone, knowing S would prove nothing about E (that would be affirming the consequent).

steps.title: Test each choice against ¬E
steps.text: A asserts E — the direct opposite of the valid inference. C invents 'partially enforceable', a category the stimulus never defines. D adds facts about intent that appear nowhere. E denies that a conclusion exists when modus tollens plainly yields one.

steps.title: The valid conclusion
steps.text: B — the contract is not enforceable — is exactly ¬E, the modus tollens conclusion. B is correct.

guides.method: Name the term-shift between evidence and conclusion

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A flaw question ('most vulnerable to the criticism'). Before reading the choices, pin down exactly what the critics claimed and exactly what the editor's evidence measures — flaw answers usually live in the gap between two near-synonyms.

steps.title: Map the exchange
steps.text: The critics' claim and the editor's rebuttal are talking past each other. Put each on the board and label what each one is actually about.

nodes.text: Critics: the policy will reduce the DIVERSITY OF VIEWPOINTS we publish.
Editor: the SUBMISSION RATE has not dropped since the policy took effect.
Editor: so the critics are mistaken.

steps.title: Spot the switched measure
steps.text: The critics predicted a drop in one quantity (variety of viewpoints); the editor rebuts with a different quantity (number of submissions). The same pile of submissions could shrink in variety while holding steady in volume — the rebuttal never touches the critics' actual claim. That mismatch of terms is the flaw to find in the choices.

rules.note: Equivocation between two different measures.

steps.title: Match the flaw
steps.text: E states it exactly: the editor confuses the volume of submissions with the diversity of viewpoints within them. A and D describe conditional and sampling errors the argument never makes, B overstates the critics' premise, and C is a harmless side fact.

guides.method: Find the causal leap, then name it

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A flaw question over a causal claim. When the evidence is a comparison between two groups and the conclusion says 'X causes Y', ask what ELSE could differ between the groups.

steps.title: Map the argument
steps.text: One correlational premise carries the whole causal conclusion — with an unstated assumption doing the real work.

nodes.text: Breakfast-eaters outperform breakfast-skippers on morning cognitive tests.
(Unstated) Nothing else about breakfast-eaters explains their scores.
Eating breakfast CAUSES improved cognitive performance.

steps.title: Generate rival explanations
steps.text: People who eat breakfast may also sleep more regularly, exercise, or differ in a dozen other ways — any of which could drive the test scores. The argument moves from 'correlated' to 'causes' without ruling any of these out. Look for the choice that names that move, not a peripheral quibble.

steps.title: Match the flaw
steps.text: C says it directly: the argument infers causation from correlation without ruling out alternative explanations. A, B, D, and E each poke at side issues — representativeness, definitions, test variety, exceptions — none of which is the load-bearing error.

guides.method: Absence of evidence vs. evidence of absence

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A flaw question. Watch what the columnist's premise actually establishes: not that the supporters are wrong — only that they haven't documented their claim.

steps.title: Map the argument
steps.text: Notice the strength mismatch between premise and conclusion.

nodes.text: Supporters have produced NO architectural surveys backing their preservation claim.
Therefore the ordinance WILL NOT preserve the historic character.

steps.title: Name the pattern
steps.text: From 'the claim is unproven' the columnist concludes 'the claim is false.' But an undocumented claim can still be true — the ordinance's actual effect is untouched by whether anyone filed a survey. Arguing from a lack of evidence to the falsity of a claim is the appeal-to-ignorance pattern.

rules.note: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

steps.title: Match the flaw
steps.text: D — treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence — is exactly the move. A (circularity), B (small sample), C (division), and E (popularity) describe fallacies the columnist never commits.

guides.method: Find what makes an elimination argument airtight

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'Depends on which assumption' is a NECESSARY-assumption question: the credited answer is something the argument cannot live without. Test candidates by negating them — if the negation wrecks the argument, you've found it.

steps.title: Symbolize the lawyer's logic
steps.text: The lawyer lists two routes to a win, eliminates one, and concludes the other must be the route.

rules.rule_text: To win, show misapplication or improper instruction.
rules.note: M = statute misapplied, I = jury improperly instructed.
Eliminate M from the disjunction… if the list was complete.

steps.title: Probe the hidden premise
steps.text: The elimination only goes through if M and I were the ONLY grounds for winning. Negate that: suppose some third ground existed — then a win would no longer guarantee improper instructions, and the conclusion collapses. That exhaustiveness is what the argument depends on.

steps.title: Match the assumption
steps.text: A — there are no other grounds on which the appeal could be won — is the necessary assumption. B and D assert outcomes the argument never needs, C confuses sufficiency with the stated necessity, and E is idle commentary about which ground was stronger.

guides.method: Strengthen a causal claim by protecting the comparison

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A strengthen question. First find the argument's weakest joint; the credited answer will brace exactly that joint, not add applause.

steps.title: Map the argument
steps.text: A group comparison feeding a causal conclusion — the classic setup where group comparability is the hidden load-bearing wall.

nodes.text: Patients on the new therapy recovered faster than patients on the standard treatment.
(Unstated) The two groups were alike apart from the therapy.
The new therapy is more effective.

steps.title: Attack yourself, then defend
steps.text: The obvious rival story: the new-therapy patients were simply younger or healthier to begin with. A strengthener that closes THAT door — showing the groups matched on age, health, and severity — converts the raw comparison into real evidence of effectiveness. Cost, seniority, and side effects don't touch the causal joint.

steps.title: Match the strengthener
steps.text: C — the groups were similar in age, overall health, and severity — rules out the selection story and most strengthens the argument. A and E are about cost and side effects, D is an appeal to the researcher's résumé, and B if anything muddies the comparison.

guides.method: Translate 'only', then chain the contrapositive

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A must-be-true question over two quantified statements. 'Only X may do Y' is the classic trap wording — translate it into an arrow before judging anything.

steps.title: Translate both statements
steps.text: 'Only employees who completed the course may operate' makes completion a REQUIREMENT of operating — the arrow starts at 'operate'.

rules.note: 'Only' introduces the necessary condition.
Always write it — it's usually the working form.

rules.rule_text: No temporary worker completed the course.

steps.title: Chain the arrows
steps.text: Link the second premise into the contrapositive: temp → ¬completed → ¬operate. Every temporary worker is barred from the forklift. Note what you may NOT infer: completion being necessary doesn't make it sufficient, so nothing follows about who DOES operate.

steps.title: Match the conclusion
steps.text: E — no temporary worker may operate the forklift — is the chained result. A contradicts it, B and D read the necessary condition as sufficient, and C reverses the first conditional.

guides.method: Check which way the arrow was fired

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A flaw question over a conditional. Symbolize the rule, then check whether the critic argued WITH the arrow (valid) or AGAINST it (flaw).

steps.title: Symbolize the critic's argument
steps.text: Lay the rule and the observation side by side and watch the direction of inference.

rules.rule_text: If a film is a commercial success, it will be widely imitated.
The comedy has spawned a dozen imitators.
rules.note: The CONSEQUENT is what was observed.
The critic drove backwards up the arrow.

steps.title: Name the pattern
steps.text: From success → imitated plus 'imitated', nothing follows — imitation could have other causes (a striking style, a cheap formula). Concluding 'success' from the consequent is affirming the consequent. Contrast the valid forms: modus ponens fires on the ANTECEDENT; modus tollens fires on the NEGATED consequent.

steps.title: Match the flaw
steps.text: B captures it: the critic treats a result that success would produce as if it established success. A describes the necessary/sufficient confusion run the other way, and C, D, and E raise sampling, generalization, and merit issues that aren't the operative error.

guides.method: Build the bridge premise

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'Follows logically if assumed' is a SUFFICIENT-assumption question: find the missing premise that makes the argument deductively valid. Mechanically: symbolize the rule and the conclusion, and see what bridges them.

steps.title: Lay out what's given and what's wanted
steps.text: One universal rule, one conclusion about Dana — the gap is glaring once symbolized.

rules.rule_text: Anyone who understands the proof will pass.

rules.note: What single fact would let the rule fire on Dana?

steps.title: Fire the rule on Dana
steps.text: The rule fires only when its antecedent holds. Feed it 'Dana understands the proof' and modus ponens delivers the conclusion outright. Anything probabilistic ('most'), reversed (pass → understand), or off-trigger (study habits) fails to guarantee it.

steps.title: Match the bridge
steps.text: A — Dana understands the proof — completes the deduction. B is off-trigger, D is merely probable, and C and E reverse the conditional, which never licenses the inference.

guides.method: Chain the conditionals, then fire modus ponens

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A must-be-true question with two linked conditionals and one fact. Chain first, fire second.

steps.title: Symbolize and link
steps.text: The consequent of the first rule is the antecedent of the second — they weld into one long arrow.

rules.rule_text: If the witness is credible, the alibi holds.
If the alibi holds, the defendant was not at the scene.

rules.note: One arrow from credibility to absence from the scene.
The witness is credible.

steps.title: Fire the chain
steps.text: The given fact is the chain's trigger: C fires C → A (the alibi holds), which fires A → ¬S. Both intermediate and final links are now established — the defendant was not at the scene.

steps.title: Match the conclusion
steps.text: A — the defendant was not at the scene — is the chained modus ponens result. B and C contradict premises, E contradicts the valid conclusion, and D reverses the chain, which is never licensed.

guides.method: Symbolize the rule, then fire modus ponens

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A 'properly concluded' question over one conditional and one fact. The only valid moves are modus ponens (the fact matches the antecedent) and modus tollens (the fact negates the consequent) — symbolize and check which applies.

steps.title: Translate the rule and the fact
steps.text: Write the arrow, its contrapositive, and the given fact — then compare the fact against the arrow's left side.

rules.note: Valid to infer; the converse (Q → P) and inverse (¬P → ¬Q) are NOT.

guides.method: Map the passage's structure, then match the thesis

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: Main-point questions reward structure over detail. Before evaluating choices, reconstruct what each paragraph does — the thesis is usually the through-line, not any single sentence.

steps.title: Map the paragraphs
steps.text: Four paragraphs, one arc: problem → failed fix → deliberate solution → modern contest. The load-bearing move is in paragraph 3: the drafters knowingly traded predictability for access.

paragraphs.gist: Writ-system pleading punished procedural missteps; the Field Code was a partial remedy.
Fact pleading bred its own pathologies; Clark's generation urged mere fair notice.
The 1938 Rules deliberately traded doctrinal predictability for procedural access; Conley cemented it.
Twombly/Iqbal's plausibility threshold — defenders and critics contest whether the bargain is being unwound.

steps.title: State the main point in your own words
steps.text: Something like: the move from rigid pleading to notice pleading was a conscious trade — predictability sacrificed for access — and that bargain is still contested. Now hunt for the choice that captures BOTH halves of the trade.

steps.title: Discard the overreaches
steps.text: A says courts 'always' preferred bright-line rules — extreme and unsupported. B claims all barriers were eliminated — paragraph 4 contradicts it. C says drafters 'rejected' the common-law tradition — too strong; they were informed by it. D equates Twombly/Iqbal with full nineteenth-century restoration — the passage says only 'partial'.

steps.title: The choice with both halves
steps.text: E — the shift reflected a deliberate trade of doctrinal predictability for procedural access — matches the paragraph-3 thesis and the arc of the whole map. E is correct.

guides.method: Read tone from the hedges, not the topic

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: An author-attitude question. Attitude lives in evaluative language — concessions, hedges, worry words — not in the subject matter. Collect the author's actual verbs about Twombly and Iqbal before rating the temperature.

steps.title: Locate the attitude paragraph
steps.text: Your structure map says the modern cases live in the final paragraph — that's where the author's stance shows.

paragraphs.gist: Presents defenders' rationale (unforeseen discovery abuses) AND critics' fear ('risk reintroducing the very access barrier…'), with the author airing both.

steps.title: Weigh the hedges
steps.text: The author grants the cases responded to real problems, yet chooses loaded framing for the downside — 'risk reintroducing the very access barrier the 1938 drafters set out to dismantle.' That is neither cheerleading nor hostility: it's a measured worry with concessions attached. Calibrate the temperature: moderate, negative-leaning, hedged.

steps.title: Match the temperature
steps.text: C — qualified concern — matches a concession-plus-worry stance. A and B are the extremes the hedging rules out, D is contradicted by the author caring enough to flag the risk, and E invents confusion the passage never displays.

guides.method: Locate, verify, and beware neighboring dates

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'According to the passage' plus a specific fact = a detail question. Do not answer from memory — locate the line, because detail questions bait you with other numbers that appear nearby in the text.

steps.title: Know where facts live
steps.text: Your paragraph map says dates and rule history live in paragraph 3 (adoption era) and paragraph 4 (modern cases). Go to paragraph 3 for the Rules' effective date.

paragraphs.gist: Fact pleading's pathologies; Clark's notice-pleading idea.
Original Federal Rules take effect; Rule 8(a)(2); Conley v. Gibson (1957).

steps.title: Disarm the decoys
steps.text: 1848 belongs to the Field Code (paragraph 1) — and 1948 echoes it. 1957 is Conley v. Gibson, the case that later cemented the standard. 1966 and 1975 appear nowhere in the passage. Every decoy is a real number from the wrong sentence.

steps.title: Read the line itself
steps.text: Paragraph 3 states the original Federal Rules 'took effect in 1938.' A is correct.

guides.method: Ask what work the detail does for the author

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'Primarily in order to' asks for the detail's FUNCTION, not its content. The answer describes what the mention accomplishes in the author's structure — so the structure map, not the sentence alone, decides it.

steps.title: Place the detail in the arc
steps.text: The Field Code appears at the hinge between paragraph 1 (problem) and paragraph 2 (the fix's own failure). It is introduced as a 'partial remedy' — and the very next paragraph opens with fact pleading generating 'its own pathologies'.

paragraphs.gist: Writ system punishes missteps; Field Code of 1848 offered a partial remedy (fact pleading).
Fact pleading generated its own pathologies — setting up the notice-pleading idea.

steps.title: Phrase the function yourself
steps.text: The Field Code's job in the passage: show an early reform that fixed part of the problem but created new ones — a stepping stone that motivates the next reform. Look for a choice saying exactly that, at that temperature.

steps.title: Discard the wrong temperatures
steps.text: A reverses the author's stance (nothing says fact pleading beat notice pleading). C inflates one example into a leadership claim. D contradicts the passage — the writ system WAS replaced. E turns one bumpy reform into 'reform inevitably fails', far beyond the author's measured tone.

steps.title: The matching function
steps.text: B — illustrate an early reform effort that solved some problems but introduced new ones — is precisely the stepping-stone role the map shows. B is correct.

guides.method: Attribute the view to the right speaker

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: An inference question about what DEFENDERS of the cases believe — not the author, not the critics. Misattribution is the trap: find the one sentence the passage puts in the defenders' mouths and stay inside it.

steps.title: Locate the defenders' sentence
steps.text: Paragraph 4 assigns each camp exactly one position — keep them separate on your map.

paragraphs.gist: Defenders: mass-tort and antitrust complaints created discovery abuses the 1938 drafters could not have foreseen. Critics: the new standard risks restoring the old access barrier.

steps.title: Paraphrase the defenders' logic
steps.text: Their point: litigation changed after 1938 in ways that produced abuse, so the old permissive standard no longer fits — newer conditions justify a tougher threshold. The right answer will restate that modest claim; wrong answers will overshoot it (abolish notice pleading, condemn Conley) or smuggle in claims about litigants the defenders never made.

steps.title: Match the inference
steps.text: D — changes in litigation since 1938 justify a more demanding pleading standard — is the direct paraphrase. A and C overshoot into abolition and retroactive error, B smears pro se litigants without textual basis, and E resurrects the Field Code, which nobody in paragraph 4 endorses.
